EXPOSE

EXPOSE [name | (name)]...

rexxref: Keyword Instructions > EXPOSE

Deviations: D70

EXPOSE lets a method use the variables that belong to its object. A method starts with no variables but its own, and the variables it sets are gone when it returns. The names that EXPOSE lists are the object's: they keep their values from one method call to the next, and every method of the object that exposes the same name sees the same variable. This page specifies which variables a name shares, the forms of the names, the one place where EXPOSE may stand, and the errors. The stems and compound names are those of the variables chapter, and the forms of the names are those of PROCEDURE, which does the same for the routine of a caller.

Object variables

[instr.expose.object]

A name that EXPOSE lists is a variable of the object that received the message, not of the method call. The method reads its value, an assignment changes it, and DROP unsets it, all for the object, so the effect outlasts the call and other methods and later calls see it. A name that is not listed is a variable of the call: it starts unset, and it is gone when the method returns. Two objects of one class have separate object variables. A name that no method has set is unset in the object, and a method that exposes it finds it unset.

c = .counter~new
c~inc; c~inc
say c~get c~peek
d = .counter~new
say d~get
::class counter
::method init
  expose n
  n = 0
::method inc
  expose n
  n += 1
  scratch = 'gone'
::method get
  expose n
  return n
::method peek
  return symbol('n') symbol('scratch')

[instr.expose.scope]

The object variables of one object are divided by the class that defines the method. Methods of one class that expose a name share a variable, and a method of a subclass that exposes the same name has a variable of its own, for the same object. A method inherited from a class works on the variables of that class.

o = .sub~new
say o~setBase('base') o~setSub('sub')
say o~getBase o~getSub

  expose v
  return v
::class sub subclass base
::method setSub

  v = arg(1)
  return 'set'
::method getSub
  expose v
  return v

[instr.expose.callee]

The variables of a method are visible to what the method runs in its own code. The text of an INTERPRET sees the exposed names, and so does an internal routine that a CALL starts without PROCEDURE. A routine that begins with PROCEDURE sees none of them unless it exposes them with PROCEDURE EXPOSE.

  return

  a = a'+h'
  return
::method after

  return a

The names

[instr.expose.stem]

A stem symbol, a name that ends in a period, exposes the whole stem of the object: every compound variable of it, those that are set and those that are set later, and the stem's default value. A compound variable such as b.1 that the method uses without exposing the stem is the method's own.

o = .box~new
say o~setup
say o~look

::method setup
  expose b.
  b.1 = 'one'
  b. = 'dflt'
  b.2 = 'two'
  return 'set'
::method look
  expose b.
  return b.1 b.2 b.9

[instr.expose.compound]

A compound symbol exposes the one variable that it names. Its tail is replaced by the value that the tail variable has when the EXPOSE runs. A tail variable is the method's own, and it has the value of the object only if the same clause has exposed it before. A later change of the tail variable does not move the exposed name, and a compound name with another tail is a variable of the method.

o = .box~new
say o~setup
say o~run
say o~look

::method setup
  expose i a.
  i = 1; a.1 = 'one'; a.2 = 'two'
  return 'set'
::method run
  expose i a.i
  say a.i
  i = 2
  say a.i
  a.i = 'local'
  return a.1 a.2 i
::method look
  expose a.
  return a.1 a.2

The list form

[instr.expose.list]

A name in parentheses is read as the list form of PROCEDURE reads it, with the string value of the DROP list, and what differs in a method is the target: the variable that holds the list is exposed first, so it is an object variable and the list is its value in the object, and each word of the list names an object variable. A list that is empty or all whitespace exposes the variable that holds it and nothing else.

o = .box~new
say o~setup
say o~run
say o~setBlank o~blank

  lst = 'x z.'

  x = 'x set'
  return symbol('x') symbol('y') symbol('z.1') symbol('lst')
::method setBlank
  expose lst
  lst = '  '
  return 'set'
::method blank
  expose (lst)

Where EXPOSE may appear

[instr.expose.first]

EXPOSE must be the first instruction of the code of a method. Only comments and null clauses may come before it in the method, so a label does not, and neither does another instruction (a NOP, a USE or a second EXPOSE included), and a position inside a DO, an IF or a SELECT is not the first. A misplaced EXPOSE raises SYNTAX 99.907 when the program is read, so no clause of the program runs. The text of an INTERPRET raises SYNTAX 99.908 when the INTERPRET runs, whether or not the method started with an EXPOSE. A program that reads the same source with .method~new shows the code, because the error is raised at that call.

say 'before'
::method m
  nop
  expose a

call try 'expose a'
call try '/* c */ ; expose a'
call try 'nop; expose a'
call try 'use arg a; expose b'
call try 'expose a; expose b'
call try 'x: expose a'
call try 'do 1; expose a; end'
call try 'if 1 then expose a'
call try 'interpret "expose a"'
call try 'return 1; expose a'
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  m = .method~new('m', arg(1))
  say arg(1) '=> ok'
  return
e: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

expose a => ok
/* c */ ; expose a => ok
nop; expose a => 99.907
use arg a; expose b => 99.907
expose a; expose b => 99.907
x: expose a => 99.907
do 1; expose a; end => 99.907
if 1 then expose a => 99.907
interpret "expose a" => ok
return 1; expose a => 99.907

o = .box~new
signal on syntax name e
o~run
e: say condition('o')~code
::class box
::method run
  interpret 'expose a'

99.908
[instr.expose.method]

EXPOSE belongs to a method. As the first instruction of the main program, or of a routine of a ::ROUTINE directive, it is accepted when the program is read and raises SYNTAX 98.992 when it runs. Anywhere else in the main program or in a routine it is misplaced, as the rule on the first instruction says, and raises 99.907 when the program is read. That includes the first clause after the label of an internal routine, also of one that a method calls, since a label does not start the code of a method.

say 'not run'
nop
expose a

expose a

say 'not run'
exit
r:
  expose a
  return

signal on syntax name e
r = .routine~new('r', 'expose a')
r~call
e: say condition('o')~code

98.992

Errors

[instr.expose.syntax]

A fault in the form of the clause is raised when the program is read, so no clause runs: 20.902 for an EXPOSE with no name and for text where a name should be, such as a string, a comma or an =; 20.906 for an empty parenthesis; 46.1 for two names in one parenthesis; 46.901 for a parenthesis that is not closed; and 31.2 or 31.3 for a name that starts with a digit or a period. The text of an INTERPRET raises the errors when the INTERPRET runs.

call try 'expose'
call try 'expose "a"'
call try 'expose a, b'
call try 'expose a = 1'
call try 'expose ()'
call try 'expose (a b)'
call try 'expose (a'
call try 'expose 3a'
call try 'expose .a'
call try 'expose a+b'
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  m = .method~new('m', arg(1))
  say arg(1) '=> ok'
  return
e: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

expose a, b => 20.902
expose a = 1 => 20.902

expose (a b) => 46.1

expose 3a => 31.2
expose .a => 31.3

Deviations

[instr.expose.deviation.70]

When a clause holds both parenthesised lists and other names, EXPOSE processes every name and every list from left to right, so a variable that an earlier name has exposed is already the object's when a later list's own variable is read. ooRexx processes the parenthesised lists first, in reverse order, and then the other names, so the variable of a list is read before any name of the clause is exposed. In the example, ooRexx reads a.i while i is still the method's own unset variable, and so exposes another name than x.

o = .box~new
say o~setup
say o~run
::class box
::method setup
  expose i a. x
  i = 1; a.1 = 'x'; x = 'X'
  return 'set'
::method run
  expose i (a.i)
  return symbol('x')

set
VAR

FORWARD

FORWARD [TO expr] [MESSAGE expr] [ARGUMENTS expr | ARRAY (expr, ...)] [CLASS expr] [CONTINUE]

rexxref: Keyword Instructions > FORWARD

FORWARD sends again the message that started the running method, with parts of it changed: the object that receives it, the name, the arguments, or the class where the search for the method starts. It is the way for a method to hand its work to another object or to the method it overrides. Without CONTINUE the running method is over once the message has been sent, and the answer of the forwarded message is the answer of the first one. This page specifies the options, what is kept of the original message, what comes back and where errors go, the places where FORWARD may stand, and the errors of the clause.

The message that is sent

[instr.forward.options]

The options may come in any order, and each may be given once. TO gives the object that receives the message, and without it the receiver is the object that received the original message. MESSAGE gives the name of the message, which is its string value made upper case, and without it the name is the one of the original message. ARGUMENTS gives the arguments, and ARRAY gives them as a list of expressions in parentheses, where an expression left out is an argument that is left empty, and without both the arguments are the ones the original message had. CLASS gives a class at which the search for the method starts, so that the methods of the classes below it are passed over, and without it the search starts at the class of the receiver. CONTINUE is described by its own rule. TO, MESSAGE, ARGUMENTS and CLASS are followed by a literal string, a constant symbol such as a number, an environment symbol such as .nil, or an expression in parentheses. A variable symbol there is not enough.

f = .front~new
say f~hello('x', 'y')
say f~named('p', 'q')
say f~mixed('p', 'q')
say f~withArgs('z')
say f~withArray
say f~noArgs('k')
::class target
::method hello
  return 'hello' arg() arg(1) arg(2)
::method recv
  s = arg()
  do i = 1 to arg()
    if arg(i, 'E') then s = s i'='arg(i)
    else s = s i'=-'
  end
  return s
::class front
::method init
  expose t
  t = .target~new
::method hello
  expose t
  forward to (t)
::method named
  expose t
  forward to (t) message 'hello'
::method mixed
  expose t
  forward message 'HeLLo' to (t)
::method withArgs
  expose t
  forward to (t) message 'recv' arguments (.array~of('A1', 'A2', 'A3'))
::method withArray
  expose t
  forward to (t) message 'recv' array ('R1', , 'R3')
::method noArgs
  expose t
  forward to (t) message 'recv' array ()

hello 2 p q
hello 2 p q
3 1=A1 2=A2 3=A3

The NIL object => 97.1
[instr.forward.nullname]

A message name that is the null string is accepted, whether it is written as a literal such as ('') or comes from a variable that holds the null string. The message with that name takes exactly one argument and answers the string value of the receiver followed by the string value of that argument. A FORWARD that sends it with no argument raises SYNTAX 93.903, and one that sends it with two or more raises 93.902, so the literal and the variable behave alike and only the number of arguments decides. Because the forwarding method has ended, a trap in the method does not see the error: the sender of the original message does. With CONTINUE the method is still running, and its own trap sees it. The arguments are those that the rule for the original message names unless ARGUMENTS or ARRAY gives others.

call try '.box~new~lit'
call try ".box~new~lit('a')"
call try ".box~new~var('b')"
call try ".box~new~lit('a', 'b')"
call try '.box~new~var'
call try ".box~new~later('c')"
call try ".box~new~later('c', 'd')"
call try '.box~new~later'
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  interpret 'say arg(1) "=>" 'arg(1)
  return
e: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

::method string
  return 'B'
::method lit
  forward message ('')
::method var
  s = ''
  forward message (s)
::method later
  signal on syntax name e
  forward message ('') continue
  return 'after' result
e: return 'in method' condition('o')~code

.box~new~lit => 93.903
.box~new~lit('a') => Ba
.box~new~var('b') => Bb
.box~new~lit('a', 'b') => 93.902
.box~new~var => 93.903
.box~new~later('c') => after Bc
.box~new~later('c', 'd') => in method 93.902
.box~new~later => in method 93.903
[instr.forward.original]

When the arguments are not given, the forwarded message carries the arguments that the original message had when the method was entered, in the same positions, with the positions that the caller left empty still empty. The method's own variables do not change that: an assignment to a variable that USE ARG filled does not change what is forwarded. When no receiver is given, the message goes to the object itself, so a name or a class that differs from the original is needed to stop the message from coming back to the method. A FORWARD that sends the same message to the same object with the same class again sends the original message unchanged, so the method runs again and forwards again; what happens then is not specified.

say d~holes(, 'two', , 'four')
say d~keepOrig('orig1', 'orig2')

  return s

::method holes

::method keepOrig

  a = 'changed'
  forward message 'recv'
::method viaSelf

[instr.forward.arguments]

The value of ARGUMENTS is turned into the list of arguments by sending it the message MAKEARRAY, so an array supplies its items, an empty array no argument, and an item that is missing in an array is an argument that is left empty. A string that is not null and has no line ends is one argument, the null string supplies none, a string of several lines has one argument for each line, and a list supplies its items. A value that cannot be made into an array raises SYNTAX 98.946.

call try 'list', .list~of(1, 2)
call try 'nil', .nil
call try 'object', .object~new
exit

  return

[instr.forward.class]

CLASS is the class at which the search for the method starts, so a method of the receiver's own class, or of a class between, is passed over when the class named is above it. The class must be one that the receiver is an instance of: the class of the receiver itself, one of its superclasses or a mixin class that it inherits. A class of the program that the receiver does not belong to raises SYNTAX 93.957, and a value that is not a class raises SYNTAX 88.914. A common use is forward class (super) to run the method that the running one overrides.

What comes back

[instr.forward.end]

Without CONTINUE the running method ends when the message has been sent, so the clauses after the FORWARD do not run. The answer of the forwarded message is the answer of the original message, and when it has none the original has none. A condition that the forwarded message raises is raised in the caller of the method, not in the method: a trap in the method does not see it. If the receiver has no method of that name, the message is an error in the caller in the same way.

d = .d~new
say d~answer
signal on syntax name e
say d~plain
say 'not reached'
e: say 'caller saw' condition('o')~code
::class d
::method answer
  forward to ('abcde') message 'length'
  say 'not run'
::method plain
  signal on syntax name h
  forward to ('abc') message 'nosuch'
  say 'not run'
h: return 'method trapped'

5
caller saw 97.1
[instr.forward.continue]

With CONTINUE the running method does not end: it goes on with the clause after the FORWARD when the forwarded message has been answered. The answer is assigned to RESULT, and when the message has no answer RESULT is dropped, as after a message instruction. A condition that the forwarded message raises is raised in the running method, where a trap can see it. The running method returns its own value, as any method does.

d = .d~new
say d~after
say d~dropped
say d~trapped
::class d
::method after
  forward to ('abc') message 'reverse' continue
  return 'after:' result
::method none
  return
::method dropped
  forward message 'none' continue
  return 'result is' symbol('result')
::method trapped
  signal on syntax name h
  forward to ('abc') message 'nosuch' continue
  return 'not reached'
h: return 'method trapped' condition('o')~code

Where FORWARD may appear

[instr.forward.method]

FORWARD works in the code of a method, anywhere among its own clauses, in a DO, an IF or a SELECT as well. In the main program, in a routine of a ::ROUTINE directive and in an internal routine, including one that a method calls, it raises SYNTAX 98.947 when it runs. The text of an INTERPRET raises SYNTAX 99.923 when the INTERPRET runs, so no clause of the text runs.

say o~deep
call try 'main'
call try 'internal'
call try 'routine'
say 'inside =>' o~inside
exit

  if what = 'internal' then do; call lab; return; end
  if what = 'routine' then call r
  say what '=> ok'
  return
e: say what '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

  forward to ('abc') message 'length'

    if 1 then forward to ('abcd') message 'length'
  end
  return 'never'
::method inside
  signal on syntax name h
  interpret "forward to ('abc') message 'length'"
  return 'no'
h: return condition('o')~code

Errors of the clause

[instr.forward.syntax]

A fault in the form of the clause is raised when the program is read. An option given twice raises SYNTAX 25.917 for TO, 25.922 for MESSAGE, 25.921 for CLASS, 25.919 for CONTINUE, and 25.918 for ARGUMENTS and ARRAY together or either one twice. A word that is not an option, or an item after the last option, raises 25.916. An option with no expression raises 35.925 for TO, 35.927 for MESSAGE, 35.926 for ARGUMENTS, 35.928 for CLASS and 35.924 for ARRAY, which also needs its expressions in parentheses. A variable symbol where an expression is wanted raises 35.1, and a parenthesis that is not closed 36.901. FORWARD with no option at all is accepted.

GUARD

GUARD ON | OFF [WHEN expression [, expression]...]

rexxref: Keyword Instructions > GUARD

A method of an object can run on several activities at once, for instance when it was started with ~start. GUARD controls whether a running method has exclusive use of its object's variables, and it can make the method wait until an object variable has a given value. This page specifies the exclusion, the WHEN form and its conditions, the places where GUARD may stand, and the errors. Which methods start guarded or unguarded is the matter of the ::METHOD directive. The EXPOSE of the variables that a WHEN expression reads is the EXPOSE instruction.

The page says only what the instruction guarantees. The order in which activities that are not held apart by a guard or by a wait make progress is not specified. Every example below is arranged so that its output does not depend on it.

Exclusion

[instr.guard.exclusion]

While an activity runs a method of an object with the guard held, no other activity runs a method of that object that also holds the guard. A method that is guarded starts with the guard held and keeps it until it ends or gives it up, and a method that is unguarded starts without it. GUARD ON takes the guard for the rest of the method, waiting until the activity that holds it has released it. GUARD OFF gives it up for the rest of the method, or until the next GUARD ON. An unguarded method can read and write the object variables without it, so it can be called while another activity holds the guard. Whether repeated GUARD ON or GUARD OFF instructions count is not specified.

log = .array~new
say 'keeping the guard'
o = .vault~new(log, .true)
h = o~start('holder')
do until o~inside; end
p = o~start('probe')
o~release
h~result; p~result
say log~makeString('l', ' ')

log = .array~new
say 'giving up the guard'
o = .vault~new(log, .false)
h = o~start('holder')
do until o~inside; end
p = o~start('probe')
p~result
o~release
h~result
say log~makeString('l', ' ')
exit
::class vault
::method init
  expose log keep inside go
  use arg log, keep
  inside = .false
  go = .false
::method holder
  expose log keep inside go
  inside = .true
  if \keep then guard off
  do until go; end
  log~append('holder-end')
  return 'h'
::method probe
  expose log
  log~append('probe')
  return 'p'
::method inside unguarded
  expose inside
  return inside
::method release unguarded
  expose go
  go = .true

keeping the guard
holder-end probe
giving up the guard
probe holder-end

Note. The example starts a method that holds the guard and a second guarded method while the first still runs. The first waits for a flag that only the main program sets, so the log shows whether the second could run before the first ended. In the second run the first method gives up the guard, and the second runs at once.

[instr.guard.end]

A guard that a method holds when it ends is released with it, whether the method held it from its start, took it with GUARD ON or kept it after GUARD ON WHEN. A method that is waiting for the guard is not kept waiting by a method that has ended.

o = .box~new
a = o~start('takes')
say a~result
b = o~start('after')
say b~result
::class box
::method takes unguarded
  guard on
  return 'took the guard'
::method after
  return 'ran after'

took the guard
ran after

WHEN

[instr.guard.when]

With WHEN the instruction waits until its condition holds. While it waits it does not hold the guard, so other activities run methods of the object, and the condition is tried again once another activity changes or unsets one of the object variables it reads; when it is tried at other times is not specified. The guard is taken again before each evaluation. When the condition is true, GUARD ON WHEN goes on with the guard held, and GUARD OFF WHEN goes on without it. A condition that is true at once does not wait.

c = .gate~new
r = c~start('waiter')
c~open
say r~result
say c~state
r2 = c~start('waiter2')
c~bump
c~bump
c~bump
say r2~result
::class gate
::method init
  expose open n
  open = .false
  n = 0
::method waiter
  expose open
  guard on when open
  return 'passed'
::method open
  expose open
  open = .true
::method state
  expose open
  return open
::method waiter2
  expose n
  guard off when n >= 3
  return 'n reached' n
::method bump
  expose n
  n += 1

passed
1
n reached 3
[instr.guard.when.value]

The condition is an expression whose value must be 0 or 1, and any other value raises SYNTAX 34.902. It can be a list of expressions separated by commas, evaluated as the list of an IF is, and a value other than 0 or 1 in an expression that is evaluated raises SYNTAX 34.6.

  call try 'one', v
  call try 'two', v
  call try 'three', v
end

w = l~start('stops')
l~setn
say w~result
exit

  signal on syntax name e
  o~set(arg(2))
  say arg(1) arg(2) '=>' o~send(arg(1))
  return
e: say arg(1) arg(2) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return
::class box
::method set
  expose x
  use arg x
::method one
  expose x
  guard on when x
  return 'passed'
::method two
  expose x
  guard on when x, 1
  return 'passed'
::method three
  expose x
  guard on when 1, x
  return 'passed'
::class lazy
::method init
  expose n
  n = 0
::method setn
  expose n
  n = 1
::method stops
  expose n
  guard on when n > 0, 10 // n = 0
  return 'passed'

[instr.guard.when.exposed]

The condition must name at least one variable that the method has exposed, as a simple symbol or as a stem symbol of its own EXPOSE, or that is an object variable because of USE LOCAL; a compound symbol exposed by its name is not enough, and neither is a name that stands only inside the parentheses or only in the list they hold. Otherwise the condition has nothing to wait for, and the program raises SYNTAX 99.913 when it is read. This holds for GUARD OFF WHEN as well. The example creates methods from source text, so that the error is raised at the call.

call try 'expose x; guard on when x'
call try 'expose x; guard on when y, x'
call try 'expose x.; guard on when x.1'
call try 'use local y; guard on when x'
call try 'expose x; guard on when y'
call try 'expose x.1; guard on when x.1'
call try 'use local y; guard on when y'
call try 'guard on when 1'
call try 'expose x; guard off when y'
call try 'expose (lst); guard on when x'
call try 'expose (lst); guard on when lst'
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  m = .method~new('m', arg(1))
  say arg(1) '=> ok'
  return
e: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

expose x; guard on when x => ok
expose x; guard on when y, x => ok
expose x.; guard on when x.1 => ok
use local y; guard on when x => ok
expose x; guard on when y => 99.913
expose x.1; guard on when x.1 => 99.913
use local y; guard on when y => 99.913
guard on when 1 => 99.913
expose x; guard off when y => 99.913
expose (lst); guard on when x => 99.913
expose (lst); guard on when lst => 99.913

Note. A WHEN condition that stays false, while no other activity is able to change an object variable, never ends. What a program does then is not specified. interrexx ends it with an exit code of 120 and a message, as Deviation 20 says, where ooRexx waits for ever.

Where GUARD may appear

[instr.guard.method]

GUARD works in the code of a method. In the main program, in a routine of a ::ROUTINE directive and in an internal routine, including one that a method calls, it raises SYNTAX 99.911 when it runs. In a method it may stand anywhere in the method's own clauses, inside a DO, an IF or a SELECT as well. The text of an INTERPRET raises SYNTAX 99.912 when the INTERPRET runs, so none of its clauses run.

o = .box~new
say o~nested
say 'inside =>' o~inside
call try 'main'
call try 'internal'
call try 'routine'
exit
try:
  what = arg(1)
  signal on syntax name e
  if what = 'main' then guard on
  if what = 'internal' then do; call lab; return; end
  if what = 'routine' then call r
  say what '=> ok'
  return
e: say what '=>' condition('o')~code
  return
lab:
  guard off
  return
::routine r
  guard on
::class box
::method nested
  do 2
    guard off
  end
  if 1 then guard on
  select
    when 1 then guard off
  end
  return 'nested ok'
::method inside
  signal on syntax name h
  interpret 'guard on'
  return 'no'
h: return condition('o')~code

nested ok
inside => 99.912
main => 99.911
internal => 99.911
routine => 99.911

Errors of the clause

[instr.guard.syntax]

A fault in the form of the clause is raised when the program is read. A GUARD without ON or OFF, with another word, or with WHEN in their place raises SYNTAX 25.913. A word after ON or OFF that is not WHEN raises 25.912. A WHEN with no expression raises 35.929.

call try 'expose x; guard'
call try 'expose x; guard foo'
call try 'expose x; guard when x'
call try 'expose x; guard on x'
call try 'expose x; guard off foo'
call try 'expose x; guard on when'
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  m = .method~new('m', arg(1))
  say arg(1) '=> ok'
  return
e: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

expose x; guard => 25.913
expose x; guard foo => 25.913
expose x; guard when x => 25.913
expose x; guard on x => 25.912
expose x; guard off foo => 25.912
expose x; guard on when => 35.929

IF

IF expression [;] THEN [;] instruction [[;] ELSE [;] instruction]

ANSI: 6.3.2.14, 8.3.9; rexxref: Keyword Instructions > IF

Deviations: D39

IF runs one instruction when a test is true and, when the program says so, another when it is false. The test is an expression whose value must be 0 or 1, and each branch is a single instruction, which is a DO group when a branch needs several. The keywords THEN and ELSE end the clause they are in, so a branch may follow on the same line, as the lexical rule says. This page specifies how the test is read, which ELSE pairs with which IF, what a branch may be, and the errors. The SELECT page is the instruction for more than two branches.

What it does

[instr.if.run]

IF evaluates its expression once. When the value is 1, the instruction after THEN runs, and when it is 0, the instruction after ELSE runs, if there is one. Control then continues with the clause after the whole IF, which is after the ELSE instruction when there is an ELSE. The branch is one instruction: a second instruction on the same line or the next line is not part of it, so it runs whatever the test said. A DO group, a SELECT or another IF is a single instruction, so a branch that holds one of them can hold many clauses. THEN need not stand in the clause of the expression: the rule for THEN says where it may begin.

n = 3
if n > 2 then say 'big'; else say 'small'
if n > 5 then say 'huge'
else say 'not huge'
if n = 3 then say 'a'; say 'b'
if n = 4 then say 'c'; say 'd'
if n = 3 then do
  say 'e1'
  say 'e2'
end
else say 'no'
say 'end'

big
not huge
a
b
d
e1
e2
end
[instr.if.then]

THEN may begin a later clause than the expression. Any number of null clauses may stand between the expression and THEN, so a line end, a semicolon, blank lines and comments there do not end the IF, and a THEN on the next line belongs to the IF above it. The same holds for the WHEN of a SELECT. The null clauses after THEN are the subject of the rule for branches.

if 1
then say 'a'
if 1; then say 'b'
if 1;; then say 'c'
if 1 /* c */

  /* c2 */
then say 'd'

a
b
c
d

The value

[instr.if.value]

The value of the expression must be a string that is exactly 0 or exactly 1, with the rules that the logical operators give for their operands: 01, 1.0, a blank around the digit, the null string and every other text are refused. An IF that gets another value raises SYNTAX 34.1, and no branch runs. A value that is an object and not a string counts as the string it converts to, which the conversion rule gives: the answer of its MAKESTRING method when it has one, and the answer of its STRING method otherwise. An object that converts to 1 takes the THEN branch, and one that converts to any other string, such as .nil, raises 34.1. The test does not look at the number form: 1 + 0 and 5 - 5 are logical because they come out as 1 and 0, and 01 is not logical because it is the text 01.

call try '1 + 0'
call try '5 - 5'
call try '2'
call try '"yes"'
call try '""'
call try '1.0'
call try '01'
call try '.nil'
call try '(1 = 1)'
call try '.probe~new'
call try '.both~new'
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  interpret 'if' arg(1) 'then r = "then"; else r = "else"'
  say arg(1) '=>' r
  return
e: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return
::class probe
::method string
  return 1
::class both
::method makestring
  return 0
::method string
  return 1

1 + 0 => then
5 - 5 => else
2 => 34.1
"yes" => 34.1
"" => 34.1
1.0 => 34.1
01 => 34.1
.nil => 34.1
(1 = 1) => then
.probe~new => then
.both~new => else
[instr.if.list]

The expression can be a list of expressions separated by commas. The list is true when every expression is, and the expressions are evaluated from left to right until one is false, so the rest are not evaluated. The value of an expression of the list that is evaluated must be 0 or 1, and any other value raises SYNTAX 34.6, which is the code for the list form, where a single expression raises 34.1. WHILE takes the same list.

call try '1, f(1)'
call try '0, f(1)'
call try '1, f(0), f(1)'
call try '0, 5'
call try '1, 5'
call try '5, 1'
exit
f: say 'f('arg(1)')'; return arg(1)
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  interpret 'if' arg(1) 'then r = "then"; else r = "else"'
  say arg(1) '=>' r
  return
e: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

f(1)
1, f(1) => then
0, f(1) => else
f(0)
1, f(0), f(1) => else
0, 5 => else
1, 5 => 34.6
5, 1 => 34.6

The ELSE

[instr.if.else]

An ELSE belongs to the nearest IF before it that has a THEN instruction and no ELSE yet, so in a nested IF the first ELSE pairs with the inner IF and the second with the outer one. The ELSE may be on the line of the THEN instruction after a semicolon, or on a later line, with blank lines and comments between, since the line end after the instruction is an implied semicolon. Nothing but null clauses may stand between the THEN instruction and its ELSE: another instruction there ends the IF, and the ELSE after it has no IF and raises SYNTAX 8.2.

y = 0
do x = 1 to 0 by -1
  if x then if y then say 'both'; else say 'x only'
  else say 'x false'
end
if 0 then say 'a'

/* a comment and a blank line do not end the IF */
else say 'b'
if 1 then say 'c';; else say 'd'
call try 'if 1 then say 1; nop; else say 2'
call try 'if 1 then say 1; else say 2; else say 3'
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  interpret arg(1)
  say arg(1) '=> ok'
  return
e: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

x only
x false
b
c
if 1 then say 1; nop; else say 2 => 8.2
if 1 then say 1; else say 2; else say 3 => 8.2

What a branch is

[instr.if.branch]

The null clauses after THEN or after ELSE are passed over, as the null-clause rule says, so then; followed by a line holds that line's instruction. A branch with no instruction is an error, and the do-nothing instruction is NOP. An ELSE directly after THEN, or after THEN and null clauses, leaves the THEN without an instruction, so the ELSE has no IF waiting for it and raises SYNTAX 8.2: if 1 then ; else say 'f' raises 8.2 and the same IF with nop after THEN does not. The word ELSE after THEN, with a = next to it, is a variable assignment, as the lexical rule says. A label cannot be a branch: the label rule gives its error.

if 1 then
  ; say 'second line is the branch'
if 0 then nop; else ; say 'else branch'
if 1 then else = 5; say else
call try 'if 1 then ; else say "f"'
call try 'if 1 then nop; else say "f"'
call try 'if 1 then say 1;; else say 2'
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  interpret arg(1)
  say arg(1) '=> ok'
  return
e: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

second line is the branch
else branch
5
if 1 then ; else say "f" => 8.2
if 1 then nop; else say "f" => ok
1
if 1 then say 1;; else say 2 => ok

Errors

[instr.if.syntax]

Errors in the shape of an IF are found when the program is read, so a program that has one runs none of its clauses. An IF with no THEN raises SYNTAX 18.1. A THEN with no instruction after it raises 14.3, and an ELSE with no instruction 14.4. A THEN that no IF waits for, an ELSE with no IF, and an END or a WHEN where the instruction of a branch should be, raise the codes of a part out of place. An error in the expression is raised when the clause runs, as it is for any expression, and when a branch is not taken, its expression is not evaluated.

say 'before'
if 1 say 'no then'

call try 'if 1'
call try 'if 1 then'
call try 'if 0 then nop; else'
call try 'then say 1'
call try 'else say 1'
call try 'if 1 then end'
call try 'if 1 then when 1'
call try 'if 0 then say 1/0; else say "other branch"'
call try 'if 1/0 then say 1'
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  interpret arg(1)
  say arg(1) '=> ok'
  return
e: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

if 1 => 18.1
if 1 then => 14.3
if 0 then nop; else => 14.4
then say 1 => 8.1
else say 1 => 8.2
if 1 then end => 10.1
if 1 then when 1 => 9.1
other branch
if 0 then say 1/0; else say "other branch" => ok
if 1/0 then say 1 => 42.3

Deviations

[instr.if.deviation.39]

A label spelled THEN that stands as a clause of its own after the expression of an IF raises SYNTAX 18.1, because the IF is still waiting for its THEN. ooRexx raises 35.1 at the colon. When the then: follows the expression in the same clause, both raise 35.1.

call try 'if 1 then: say 1'
call try 'if 1; then: say 1'
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  interpret arg(1)
  say arg(1) '=> ok'
  return
e: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

if 1 then: say 1 => 35.1
if 1; then: say 1 => 18.1

INTERPRET

INTERPRET expression

ANSI: 6.3.2.62, 8.3.10; rexxref: Keyword Instructions > INTERPRET

Deviations: D51, D66, D76

INTERPRET evaluates an expression and runs the string that results as instructions, at the place where the INTERPRET stands. The instructions of the text are those of the clause's own routine, method or program: they read and assign its variables, take its arguments and use its settings. The text is program text without a file around it, so it has no lines and no labels, and it must hold only whole constructs. This page specifies what the text may hold, how it is run, how control leaves it and what errors it raises.

Running the text

[instr.interpret.run]

INTERPRET evaluates its expression, takes the string value of the result and runs it as a sequence of clauses, from the first to the last. When the last has run, the clause after the INTERPRET runs. The text may hold any instruction, including another INTERPRET, and the instruction may be written in any case, over any number of clauses separated by semicolons. The expression is an ordinary expression, so a text is often built from pieces.

slot = 'total'
interpret slot '= 6 * 7'
say total
interpret 'p = 1; q = p + 1'
say p q
interpret 'say' 1 + 1
interpret 'do 2; say "loop"; end'
interpret 'interpret "z = 9"'
say z

42
1 2
2
loop
loop
9
[instr.interpret.empty]

A text that holds no clause, because it is the null string, blanks, one or more comments or a bare semicolon, does nothing. An INTERPRET with no expression after the keyword raises SYNTAX 35.912, which a program file raises when it is read, so that it runs nothing and exits with 221. An error in the expression is raised before any text is read.

interpret ''
interpret '   '
interpret '/* only a comment */'
interpret '-- a line comment'
interpret ';'
say 'nothing happened'
signal on syntax name e
interpret 1 / 0
e: say condition('o')~code
call try 'interpret'
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name e2
  interpret arg(1)
  say 'ok' arg(1)
  return
e2: say condition('o')~code '<=' arg(1)
  return

nothing happened
42.3
35.912 <= interpret

say 'before'
interpret

Scope

[instr.interpret.scope]

The text runs in the scope of the code that holds the INTERPRET. A variable that the text sets is set for the code after the INTERPRET, a variable that the text drops is dropped, and the text reads the arguments of the routine through ARG and PARSE ARG. In a method, the text sees the object variables that the method exposed and the method's SELF. A NUMERIC setting that the text makes stays in force for the code after the INTERPRET, and so does an ADDRESS setting.

numeric digits 12
interpret 'numeric digits 5; v = 1 / 3'
say digits() v
call sub 'one', 'two'
say digits() v
o = .box~new
o~go
exit
sub:
  interpret 'say arg(1) arg(2) arg()'
  interpret 'parse arg p, q; w = p || q; numeric digits 3'
  say p q w digits()
  interpret 'drop p'
  say symbol('p') symbol('w')
return
::class box
::method init
  expose n
  n = 5
::method go
  expose n
  interpret 'n = n + 1; say n self~class~id'
  say n

one two 2
one two onetwo 3

Translation and running

[instr.interpret.whole]

The text is read as a whole before its first clause runs. An error of the kind that a program file raises when it is read, such as an expression that cannot be read, an unterminated string or comment, a label, a directive or an unbalanced construct, is raised before any clause of the text runs, so the clauses before the faulty one do nothing. An error that a clause raises when it runs, such as a zero divisor or a missing routine, is raised when that clause runs, and the clauses before it have run.

call try 'say "first"; say 2 +'
call try 'say "first"; say "open'
call try 'say "first"; say 1 2 )'
call try 'say "first"; end'
call try 'say "first"; x = 1 / 0'
call try 'say "first"; call nosuchroutine'
call try 'say "first"; signal nolabel'
call try 'say "first"; if 2 then nop'
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  interpret arg(1)
  say 'ok' arg(1)
  return
e: say condition('o')~code '<=' arg(1)
  return

[instr.interpret.lines]

The text has no line ends. A line feed or a carriage return in it, which is what a program file would read as the end of a line, raises SYNTAX 13.1 when the text is read, and so does a result that the conversion makes into several lines, such as an Array. A -- comment therefore runs to the end of the whole text and hides what follows it, even after a semicolon, and a comma at the very end of the text is accepted.

call try 'say 1' || '0a'x || 'say 2'
call try 'say 1' || '0d'x || 'say 2'
call try 'say 3 -- c; say 4'
call try 'say 5,'
call try 'interpret .array~of("say 6", "say 7")'
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  interpret arg(1)
  say 'ok' arg(1)
  return
e: say condition('o')~code
  return

[instr.interpret.complete]

Every DO, IF and SELECT that the text opens must end inside it, and the text may not hold the end of a construct that began outside it. A simple DO with no END raises SYNTAX 14.1, a SELECT with no END 14.2, and a loop with no END 14.5. An IF with no THEN raises 18.1, a THEN with no instruction after it 14.3 and an ELSE with none 14.4. An END with no construct to end is a part out of place, and so is an END that would close a loop around the INTERPRET. A THEN, an ELSE, a WHEN and an OTHERWISE with no IF or SELECT before it are too. Complete constructs run as they do in a program.

interpret 'do 2; say "a"; end'
interpret 'if 1 then say "t"; else say "e"'
interpret 'select; when 0 then say 0; otherwise say "o"; end'
signal on syntax name outer
do 2
  interpret 'end'
end

call try 'else say 1'
call try 'when 1 then say 1'
call try 'otherwise say 1'
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  interpret arg(1)
  say 'ok' arg(1)
  return
e: say condition('o')~code '<=' arg(1)
  return

[instr.interpret.labels]

The text may not hold a label or a directive. A label raises SYNTAX 47.1, as the label rule says, and a clause that starts with :: raises SYNTAX 99.914, wherever in the text it stands. Both are raised before any clause of the text runs.

call try 'say "first"; lab: say 2'
call try 'lab:'

call try 'say "first"; ::method m'
call try '::requires "x.rex"'

  signal on syntax name e

  say 'ok' arg(1)
  return

Leaving the text

[instr.interpret.transfer]

An instruction of the text that moves control moves it for the code that holds the INTERPRET. A RETURN returns from that routine or method with its value, or ends the program, and the clauses after the INTERPRET do not run. An EXIT does what it would do where the INTERPRET stands, as the EXIT rules say. In the main program and in an internal routine of it, it ends the program with its value as the exit code. In a method or a ::ROUTINE, it ends only that unit, and the value goes to the sender or the caller as the rule for a unit says. A SIGNAL to a label of the program leaves the text and any active DO, IF or SELECT, and sets SIGL to the number of the line of the INTERPRET clause, as it would for a SIGNAL written there.

say f(5)
call sub
say 'sigl' sigl result
interpret 'signal lab; say "no"'
say 'not run'
lab: say 'at lab' sigl
say 'method' .box~new~run
say 'routine' later()
interpret 'exit 3'
say 'not run'
f: interpret 'return arg(1) * 2'
say 'not run'
sub: return 'from sub'
::class box
::method run
  interpret 'exit "from method"'
  say 'not run'
::routine later
  interpret 'exit "from routine"'
  say 'not run'

[instr.interpret.result]

INTERPRET does not set RESULT and does not drop it, and an instruction of the text that sets or drops RESULT, such as a CALL, does it for the code that holds the INTERPRET.

result = 'keep'
interpret 'nop'
interpret 'z = 1'
say result
interpret 'call giver "x"'
say result
interpret 'call quiet'
say symbol('result')
exit
giver: return arg(1)'!'
quiet: return

x!

[instr.interpret.loop]

A LEAVE or ITERATE in the text refers to a loop that the text itself holds. A loop of the code around the INTERPRET is out of reach: the instruction raises SYNTAX 28.1 for a LEAVE and 28.2 for an ITERATE with no name, and 28.3 and 28.4 when the instruction names a loop, even in the body of a loop. A simple DO group is not a loop, as the LEAVE rule says. The text may not hold a PROCEDURE, an EXPOSE, a USE LOCAL, a GUARD, a FORWARD or a REPLY. Each page says what it raises there. In the example, an EXPOSE and a REPLY raise when the text is read, so that no clause of the text runs.

signal on syntax name e1
do i = 1 to 3
  say 'loop' i
  interpret 'if i = 2 then leave'
end
e1: say condition('o')~code i
signal on syntax name e2
do j = 1 to 3
  say 'loop' j
  interpret 'if j = 2 then iterate j'
end
e2: say condition('o')~code j
signal on syntax name e3
call r1
e3: say condition('o')~code
exit
r1: interpret 'procedure expose x'

Errors

[instr.interpret.error]

An error in the text is a SYNTAX condition raised at the INTERPRET clause. SIGL is the number of the line on which that clause begins, whichever line of the text the error is in and however many lines the clause spans. A program that does not trap the condition ends with the exit code that the error gives, as for any other error.

  'say 2 +'

interpret 'say 1 2 )'
e3: say condition('o')~code sigl

Deviations

[instr.interpret.deviation.76]

The condition object of a SYNTAX error that arises while the text is translated names the package that holds the INTERPRET. The object that its PACKAGE method answers is the one that .context~package answers in the code. In ooRexx the object is another package that has the same name.

signal on syntax name e

e: c = condition('o')
say c~code (c~package == .context~package)

[instr.interpret.deviation.51]

Inside the text, .RS and .CONTEXT~RS answer the same value: the return code that a command in the text has just set. In ooRexx the method answers the value that the caller had before the INTERPRET until the text ends, and .RS answers the new value at once.

say .rs .context~rs

[instr.interpret.deviation.66]

A trap that SIGNAL ON enabled, and whose label does not exist, raises SYNTAX 16.1 when its condition occurs, as the conditions chapter specifies. When the condition occurs in the text of an INTERPRET, the condition has one stack frame, of the type PROGRAM, and its name is the name of the program. In ooRexx the name of that frame is the null string.

ITERATE

ITERATE [name]

ANSI: 6.3.2.63, 8.3.11; rexxref: Keyword Instructions > ITERATE

ITERATE ends the current pass of a loop and starts the next one. The rest of the block does not run for that pass. The loop then does the work that ends a pass: the step, the tests, and the next pass. Without a name it acts on the innermost loop that is running, and with a name on the loop that has that name, which can be one further out. This page specifies what the next pass begins with, which loops a name can select, and the errors. It describes loops by the terms of DO, and LEAVE is the instruction that ends the loop itself.

What it does

[instr.iterate.effect]

ITERATE does what the END of the block does. A controlled loop steps its variable and runs its end tests, a WHILE phrase is tested before the next pass, and an UNTIL phrase is tested at once, so an ITERATE can end the loop when the UNTIL holds. A COUNTER variable counts the next pass as usual. If the selected loop is not the innermost, every block open inside it is closed first, and the control variables of those blocks keep their values. The clauses after the ITERATE do not run in the pass that it ends.

do i = 1 to 3
  if i = 2 then iterate
  say 'pass' i
end
say 'after' i
do j = 1 to 5 until t(j)
  say 'body' j
  iterate
end
say 'j' j
do counter c k = 1 to 3
  iterate
end
say 'c' c 'k' k
do a = 1 to 2
  do b = 1 to 5
    if b = 2 then iterate a
    say a b
  end
end
say 'a' a 'b' b
exit
t: say 'test' arg(1); return arg(1) = 2

pass 3
after 4
body 1
test 1
body 2
test 2
j 2
c 3 k 4
1 1
2 1
a 3 b 2

Which loop it selects

[instr.iterate.target]

An ITERATE with no name selects the innermost running block that is a repetitive loop, and a simple group and a SELECT are passed over, as they are for LEAVE. With no loop to select it raises SYNTAX 28.2. A name that is the label of a simple group or of a SELECT raises SYNTAX 28.5, since a block that does not repeat has no next pass.

do 2
  do
    say 'group'
    iterate
  end
  say 'skipped'
end
do 2
  select
    when 1 then iterate
  end
  say 'skipped'
end

call try 'do label g; iterate g; end'

exit

[instr.iterate.name]

ITERATE name selects the innermost running loop whose name is name. The names are those of the LABEL rule. When no running loop has the name, ITERATE raises SYNTAX 28.4. A name that is not a symbol raises SYNTAX 20.908, and data after the name SYNTAX 21.908. Those two are found when the program is read, as the LEAVE rule says of the same faults: no clause runs, and the exit codes are 236 and 235, as the rule for a program that is read says.

Where it runs and its errors

[instr.iterate.active]

An ITERATE can only select a loop that is running in the same part of the program where it stands, in the way LEAVE states. A loop that a routine or an INTERPRET text was called out of is not running for the callee. An ITERATE with no name there raises SYNTAX 28.2, and one with a name raises 28.4. The error is raised when the clause runs, so a clause that no path reaches raises nothing.

LEAVE

LEAVE [name]

ANSI: 6.3.2.64, 8.3.12; rexxref: Keyword Instructions > LEAVE

LEAVE ends a block early. Control passes to the clause after the END of the block that it ends, as if the loop had run out of passes, and the control variable keeps the value it had. Without a name it ends the innermost repetitive loop that is running, and with a name it ends the block that has that name, which can be a block further out. This page specifies which blocks a LEAVE can end, how a name picks one, what runs and what does not, and the errors. It describes loops by the terms of DO, and ITERATE is the instruction that ends only the current pass.

What it ends

[instr.leave.effect]

LEAVE ends the block that it selects and every block that is open inside it. The clause that runs next is the one after the END of the selected block. No test of the block runs, neither a UNTIL nor a WHILE nor the end test of a controlled loop, and the control variable is not stepped, so it keeps the value that the pass had. A COUNTER variable keeps its value too. The clauses that follow the LEAVE in the block do not run. An IF, a THEN and an ELSE are not blocks that LEAVE ends, so a LEAVE in one ends the loop around it.

do i = 1 to 3
  if i = 2 then leave
  say 'pass' i
end
say 'after' i
do counter c j = 10 to 20 until j = 12
  leave
end
say c j
do a = 1 to 2
  do b = 1 to 3
    if b = 2 then leave
    say a b
  end
end
say a b
do 2
  if 1 then leave
  say 'skipped'
end
say 'out'

[instr.leave.target]

A LEAVE with no name selects the innermost block that is a repetitive loop and is running. A simple group, which is a DO with no repetitor, and a SELECT are not loops, so an unnamed LEAVE passes over them and selects the loop around them, and raises SYNTAX 28.1 when it has none. A group or a SELECT whose label a LEAVE names can be left, as can a loop.

    say 'group'
    leave

  say 'skipped'

say 'after loop'

Where it runs

[instr.leave.active]

A LEAVE can only select a block that is running in the same routine or program part where the LEAVE stands. A loop that a routine, a method or an INTERPRET text was called out of is not running for that call, so a LEAVE in the callee that has no loop of its own raises SYNTAX 28.1, and one that names a loop of the caller raises 28.3. The INTERPRET rule states the same for the text. A loop inside the callee works as usual.

do 1
  call plain
end
do label q 1
  call named
end
call inner
exit

  signal on syntax name e1
  leave
e1: say 'plain' condition('o')~code
  return
named:
  signal on syntax name e2
  leave q
e2: say 'named' condition('o')~code
  return
inner:
  do 3
    leave
  end
  say 'inner done'
  return

[instr.leave.error]

A LEAVE outside any block that it could select raises SYNTAX 28.1, and a named one raises SYNTAX 28.3. These are raised when the LEAVE runs, so the clauses before it run, and a LEAVE that no path reaches raises nothing. The two faults in the form of the clause, a name that is not a symbol (SYNTAX 20.907) and data after the name (SYNTAX 21.907, whatever the name is and whether or not a block has it), are found when the program is read instead. No clause of the program runs then, even one before the LEAVE or a LEAVE that no path reaches, and the exit code is 236 or 235, as the rule for a program that is read says. In the text of an INTERPRET the same faults are ordinary SYNTAX conditions, as the name rule shows.

say 'unreached leave is no error'

LOOP

LOOP [LABEL name] [COUNTER name] [repetitor] [conditional]; instructions; END [name]

ANSI: 6.3.2.12, 8.3.6; rexxref: Keyword Instructions > LOOP

LOOP is the repetitive form of DO under a second keyword. Every clause that follows the keyword has the same meaning that it has after DO, and the block ends at the same END. The one difference is the clause that has nothing after the keyword: a DO with nothing is a group that runs once, and a LOOP with nothing is a loop that never ends by itself. This page states that difference and the places where the keyword matters. The standard defines DO only, so LOOP is an addition of ooRexx, and the ansi citation of this page names the sections of DO.

What LOOP is

[instr.loop.same]

Every form of DO that has a repetitor or a condition has the same meaning under the keyword LOOP, and the phrases LABEL, COUNTER, TO, BY, FOR, OVER, WITH, WHILE and UNTIL are the same. The two keywords can be mixed, since LOOP and DO both start a block that ends at an END, and an END closes the nearest block of either kind. The rules of the DO page for the evaluation of the phrases, the tests, the control variable, the errors and the END symbol hold for LOOP without change. The keyword is not case sensitive.

loop 2; say 'count'; end
loop i = 1 to 2; say 'control' i; end
loop e over .array~of('p', 'q'); say 'over' e; end
loop counter c while c < 2; say 'while' c; end
loop until 1; say 'until'; end
do label a
  loop label b i = 1 to 3
    if i = 2 then leave a
    say 'mixed' i
  end b
end a
LOOP I = 1 TO 2; SAY 'upper' I; END i
signal on syntax name e1
interpret 'loop i = 1 to 2; end j'
e1: say condition('o')~code

over q

[instr.loop.forever]

A LOOP with no repetitor and no condition is an endless loop, as DO FOREVER is. A LABEL phrase alone does not make it a group: LOOP LABEL name is endless. A COUNTER phrase counts the passes of such a loop, since a LOOP with nothing but a COUNTER is allowed where a DO is not. Only a LEAVE, an EXIT, a RETURN, a SIGNAL or an error ends it.

n = 0
loop
  n = n + 1
  if n = 3 then leave
end
say n
loop label top
  n = n + 1
  if n > 4 then leave top
end top

  if c = 3 then leave
end
say c

  leave
end

[instr.loop.keyword]

LOOP is a keyword only at the start of a clause that is not an assignment. A symbol loop that an = follows is an assignment to a variable of that name, a stem or compound symbol that starts with loop is a variable, and loop(...) inside an expression is a call of a function of that name, as the keyword rule and the list of keywords say for every keyword. A LOOP clause with an opening parenthesis straight after the keyword is a loop whose count is that parenthesized expression.

Message instructions

rexxref: General Concepts > Clauses and Instructions > Message Instructions; General Concepts > Message Instructions

Deviations: D36

A message instruction is a clause that sends a message to an object for what the object does, where a message term in an expression is evaluated for what it answers. The clause is a message term with nothing after it, or a message term followed by = and an expression, which sets a value on the receiver. This page specifies how the interpreter treats the answer of a message instruction, how a message assignment is turned into a message, the order in which its parts are evaluated, and the errors. The syntax of a message term and the messages that strings and operators understand are in the expressions chapter, and the classes specify what their methods do.

The clause

[instr.message.clause]

A clause is a message instruction when it is a single message term: a term followed by one or more messages or subscripts, with no operator or other term after the last of them. The term in front may be a symbol, a string, a function call, a class name or an expression in parentheses. The message goes to the receiver by the same steps as in an expression. The kinds rule says which other clauses are commands, among them one with an operator after the message. A message instruction does not set RC, and a command does not set RESULT.

address system
o = .box~new
call t 'o~answer'
call t 'o~answer~~class'
call t '(o)~answer'
call t 'o[1]'
call t '(o~answer)'
call t "o~answer ''"
call t 'f(1)'
exit
t:
  drop result
  rc = 'unset'
  interpret arg(1)
  say left(arg(1), 16) symbol('result') rc
  return
f: return 'exit 0'
::class box
::method answer
  return 'exit 0'
::method '[]'
  return 'exit 0'

o~answer         VAR unset
o~answer~~class  VAR unset
(o)~answer       VAR unset
o[1]             VAR unset
(o~answer)       LIT 0
o~answer ''      LIT 0
f(1)             LIT 0

The answer

[instr.message.result]

After a message instruction, RESULT holds the object that the message answered, and it is dropped when the message answered nothing, so that the earlier value is gone either way. A message instruction whose last operator is ~~ answers its receiver whatever the message did, so RESULT holds the receiver. A message to a string is a message instruction like any other, so 'abc'~length sets RESULT to 3.

o = .box~new
result = 'old'
o~answer
say 'A' result
o~silent
say 'B' symbol('result') result
o~answer(1, 2)
say 'C' result
'abc'~length
say 'D' result
o~~answer
say 'E' result~class~id
o~answer~~length
say 'F' result
::class box
::method answer
  return 'ans' arg()
::method silent
  return

B LIT RESULT
C ans 2
D 3

Message assignments

[instr.message.assign]

The clause term~name = expression sends the message name=, which is the name with an equal sign added, to the value of the term. The value of the expression is the first argument. A name written as a string gets the equal sign in the same way, and the case of the name does not matter. The clause term[i, j] = expression sends the message []= the same way, with the value of the expression first and the values of the index expressions after it, and the brackets may hold no expression at all. When the message has its own arguments, as in term~name(a) = expression, the value comes first and the arguments follow. The answer of the message is treated as for any message instruction, so it is assigned to RESULT, or RESULT is dropped. A ~~ in front of the name has no effect on that, so RESULT holds what name= answered, not the receiver.

result = 'old'
o~x = 5
say 'A' result
o~"X" = 6
o~y(7, 8) = 9
say 'B' symbol('result')
o[10, 11] = 12
o[] = 13

  say 'x= got' arg() arg(1)
  return 'ignored'
::method 'y='
  say 'y= got' arg() arg(1) arg(2) arg(3)
::method '[]='
  say '[]= got' arg() arg(1)'|'arg(2)'|'arg(3)

[instr.message.assign.order]

In a message assignment the receiver term is evaluated first, then the expression after the =, and then the argument expressions of the message or of the brackets from left to right. This differs from the order of the message term in an expression, where the arguments follow the receiver directly.

n(.rec~new)~z(n(1), n(2)) = n(3)
say '--'
n(.rec~new)[n(4), n(5)] = n(6)
exit

[instr.message.assign.extended]

An extended assignment on a message term, such as term~name += expression or term[i] ||= expression, sends two messages: the term is read with name or [], the operator is applied to the answer and the value of the expression, and the result is set with name= or []=. The read is the message term as written, so with ~~ it answers the receiver and the operator is applied to the receiver itself. The receiver term is evaluated twice, both times before the read. The argument expressions of a subscript are evaluated once for the read and a second time, after the expression, for the assignment, so a term or an argument that has an effect has it twice.

n(.rec~new)~x += n(1)
say '--'
n(.rec~new)[n(2)] ||= n(3)
exit
n: say 'eval' arg(1)~class~id arg(1); return arg(1)

::method 'x'

::method '[]='
  say '[]= got' arg(1)
::method '[]'
  say '[] read' arg(1); return 100

Errors

[instr.message.error]

A message instruction whose receiver does not understand the message raises SYNTAX 97.1, and so does a message assignment, since it needs a method whose name ends in an equal sign. A message assignment with no expression after the = raises SYNTAX 35.1, not the 35.918 of an assignment to a variable. A message operator with no name raises SYNTAX 19.909, as the expression rules say. A string understands no []=, so a subscript assignment on one raises 97.1.

call try "o~nosuch"
call try "o~nosuch = 1"
call try "o~x = "
call try "o~"
call try "'abc'~foo = 1"
call try "'abc'[1] = 1"
call try "o~x += 1"
exit

  signal on syntax name e
  interpret arg(1)
e: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

In a program file, a message assignment with no expression is found when the program is read, as the expression rules say of any expression that cannot be read. The program writes nothing and exits with 221.

[instr.message.deviation.36]

A message assignment of objectName= to a string is refused and ends the program with exit code 120, because a string is value-based, as Deviation 36 says. ooRexx accepts the assignment and gives the name to the string.

NOP

NOP

ANSI: 6.3.2.65, 8.3.14; rexxref: Keyword Instructions > NOP

NOP is the instruction that does nothing. It exists for the places where the language needs an instruction and the program has nothing to do, such as a branch of an IF or a SELECT that is meant to stay empty. It takes no operand, and any data after the keyword is an error.

What it does

[instr.nop.effect]

NOP changes no variable and no special variable, writes nothing and sends nothing to an environment. A clause after it runs as if the NOP were absent, and RESULT and RC keep the values that they had. A NOP that stands as the body of a THEN, an ELSE, a WHEN or an OTHERWISE gives that branch an instruction that does nothing.

result = 'r0'; rc = 'c0'
call giver
nop
say result rc
if 1 then nop
else say 'not run'
if 0 then nop; else say 'else run'
select
  when 0 then nop
  otherwise nop
end
do 2; nop; end
say 'done'
exit
giver: return 'given'

given c0
else run
done
[instr.nop.keyword]

The word NOP starts the instruction in any case, and the clause ends where the instruction does, so a semicolon, a line end or a comment may follow it and another clause may follow on the same line. A clause that begins with nop = is an assignment to a variable of that name, and one that begins with nop.x = is an assignment to a compound variable, as the kind rule says.

Nop; NOP /* comment */ ; nop -- more
nop = 'a variable'
say nop
nop.x = 'a compound'
say nop.x

a variable
a compound

Errors

[instr.nop.error]

Anything after NOP in its clause, other than the end of the clause, raises SYNTAX 21.901: a symbol, a number, a string, a parenthesis or a keyword such as THEN. A program file raises it when the program is read, so no clause runs, and the exit code is 235. The text of INTERPRET raises it as it does any error found in reading.

say 'before'
nop 1

call try 'nop 1'
call try 'nop x'
call try 'nop "s"'
call try 'nop(1)'
call try 'nop then'
call try 'nop end'
call try 'nop'
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  interpret arg(1)
  say 'ok' arg(1)
  return
e: say condition('o')~code '<=' arg(1)
  return

21.901 <= nop 1
21.901 <= nop x
21.901 <= nop "s"
21.901 <= nop(1)
21.901 <= nop then
21.901 <= nop end
ok nop

NUMERIC

NUMERIC {DIGITS [expression] | FUZZ [expression] | FORM [SCIENTIFIC | ENGINEERING | [VALUE] expression]}

ANSI: 6.3.2.66, 8.3.15; rexxref: Keyword Instructions > NUMERIC

NUMERIC changes one of the three settings that steer arithmetic: the number of digits kept, the number of digits a comparison ignores, and the notation of an exponent. The meaning of each setting, the values it accepts, its default and the part of the program that a change reaches belong to the numeric settings, and this page does not repeat them. It specifies the syntax of the instruction, when its expression is evaluated, what leaving the expression out means, the forms of FORM, and the errors of the clause.

DIGITS and FUZZ

[instr.numeric.value]

NUMERIC DIGITS and NUMERIC FUZZ take an optional expression. The expression is an ordinary one, so it may use operators, variables and function calls, and it is evaluated before the setting changes, with the setting in force. Its value is then checked and stored as the DIGITS and the FUZZ rules say. A comma after the expression is not refused when the program is read; the clause then fails as a value that the setting does not accept, 26.5 for DIGITS and 26.6 for FUZZ. The keywords may be written in any case, and a comment may stand between the words.

numeric digits 5 + 5
say digits()
numeric digits digits() * 2
say digits()
Numeric /* now */ DIGITS 3
say digits()
numeric digits 100 + 0.4
say digits()
numeric fuzz 1 + 1
say fuzz()
signal on syntax name e
say 'before'
numeric digits 5, 6
say 'not reached'
e: say condition('o')~code digits()

10
20
3
100
2
before
26.5 100
[instr.numeric.default]

NUMERIC DIGITS or NUMERIC FUZZ with no expression returns the setting to its default, which is 9 for DIGITS and 0 for FUZZ unless the package names another one, as DIGITS and FUZZ say. The clause ends at the semicolon or the line end that follows the keyword.

numeric digits 20
numeric fuzz 3
numeric digits; numeric fuzz
say digits() fuzz()

9 0

FORM

[instr.numeric.form]

NUMERIC FORM has four shapes. The symbol SCIENTIFIC or ENGINEERING, in any case, names the form to set. The keyword VALUE followed by an expression sets the form to the value of the expression. VALUE may be left out when the first token of the expression is not a symbol, as with a string or a parenthesis. With nothing after FORM the form returns to its default. The value of an expression has to be exactly SCIENTIFIC or ENGINEERING, in capitals, with no blanks round it and no abbreviation.

numeric form engineering
say form()
numeric form Scientific
say form()
f = 'ENGINEERING'
numeric form value f
say form()
numeric form ('SCIENTIFIC')
say form()
numeric form value 'ENG' || 'INEERING'
say form()
numeric form
say form()
numeric form 'ENGINEERING'
say form()
numeric form
say form()

ENGINEERING
SCIENTIFIC
ENGINEERING
SCIENTIFIC
ENGINEERING
SCIENTIFIC
ENGINEERING
SCIENTIFIC
[instr.numeric.form.error]

A value that is not exactly one of the two words raises SYNTAX 25.11 when the instruction runs, and the form stays as it was. Lower case, mixed case, blanks round the word, an abbreviation and a number are all such values. Any other symbol directly after FORM, a variable or a number included, is refused with 25.11 when the program is read, and its value is never looked at.

call try "numeric form 'engineering'"
call try "numeric form value 'Engineering'"
call try "numeric form value ' ENGINEERING '"
call try "numeric form value 'ENG'"
call try "numeric form value 5"
call try "numeric form value nosuch"
call try "numeric form + 1"
call try "numeric form nosuch"
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  numeric form scientific
  interpret arg(1)
  say arg(1) '=>' form()
  return
e: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code form()
  return

numeric form 'engineering' => 25.11 SCIENTIFIC
numeric form value 'Engineering' => 25.11 SCIENTIFIC
numeric form value ' ENGINEERING ' => 25.11 SCIENTIFIC
numeric form value 'ENG' => 25.11 SCIENTIFIC
numeric form value 5 => 25.11 SCIENTIFIC
numeric form value nosuch => 25.11 SCIENTIFIC
numeric form + 1 => 25.11 SCIENTIFIC
numeric form nosuch => 25.11 SCIENTIFIC

nosuch = 'ENGINEERING'
say 'before'
numeric form nosuch

Errors

[instr.numeric.syntax]

A fault in the form of the clause is raised when the program is read, so no clause runs: 20.905 for NUMERIC alone or followed by something that is not a symbol; 25.15 for a symbol that is not DIGITS, FUZZ or FORM; 21.911 for anything after SCIENTIFIC or ENGINEERING; and 35.917 for FORM VALUE with no expression. A fault in the expression is the error of the expression, such as 35.1 for an operator with nothing after it. A value that the setting does not accept is raised when the instruction runs, with the error that the settings rules give: 26.5, 26.6 or 33.1. An INTERPRET raises the same errors when it runs.

say 'before'
numeric

call try 'numeric'
call try "numeric 'digits' 5"
call try 'numeric foo'
call try 'numeric forms scientific'
call try 'numeric form engineering extra'
call try 'numeric form scientific 1'
call try 'numeric form value'
call try 'numeric digits 5 +'
call try 'numeric digits 5 6'
call try 'numeric fuzz 1 2'
call try 'numeric digits nosuch'
call try 'numeric digits 0'
call try 'numeric fuzz 9'
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  numeric digits 9
  numeric fuzz 0
  interpret arg(1)
  say arg(1) '=> ok'
  return
e: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

numeric => 20.905
numeric 'digits' 5 => 20.905
numeric foo => 25.15
numeric forms scientific => 25.15
numeric form engineering extra => 21.911
numeric form scientific 1 => 21.911
numeric form value => 35.917
numeric digits 5 + => 35.1
numeric digits 5 6 => 26.5
numeric fuzz 1 2 => 26.6
