Routines of a native library

[dir.routine.external]

EXTERNAL declares a routine that a native library supplies, and the directive has no section. Its operand is a string whose first word is LIBRARY or REGISTERED, in any case, followed by the name of the library and optionally one more word, the entry in it. A missing operand, or one that is not a string, raises SYNTAX 19.905, and any other operand, such as a first word that is neither, a missing library name or more words than the entry, raises 99.917. A clause after the directive that is not a null clause raises 99.939. A library that cannot be loaded raises 98.903 for LIBRARY and 90.999 for REGISTERED, and a library that loads but has no routine of the entry name raises 90.999. These are raised when the section of the directive ends, so a clause in the section is refused first; the rule for external methods says how that order goes for the faults of other directives. The operand of the LIBRARY form is the one that ::METHOD takes. How a library is searched for, and which routine of it the declaration binds, are not specified here.

call try '::routine r external "library spec_no_such_lib_xyz"'
call try '::routine r external "Library spec_no_such_lib_xyz entry"'
call try '::routine r external "registered spec_no_such_lib_xyz"'
call try '::routine r external "registered spec_no_such_lib_xyz entry"'
call try '::routine r external "frob spec_no_such_lib_xyz"'
call try '::routine r external "library"'
call try '::routine r external "library rexxutil nosuchentry_xyz"'
call try '::routine r external library'
call try '::routine r external "library a b c"'
call try '::routine r external ""'
call try '::routine r external'
call try '::routine r external "library spec_no_such_lib_xyz"', 'say 1'
call try '::routine r external "library spec_no_such_lib_xyz"', '::frob'
call try '::frob', '::routine r external "library spec_no_such_lib_xyz"'
exit

  return
e: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code

::REQUIRES

::REQUIRES name [LIBRARY | NAMESPACE ns]

rexxref: Directives > ::REQUIRES

::REQUIRES makes the public classes and routines of another package known to this one. The other package is a Rexx program, which the interpreter installs and whose prolog it runs before the requiring package goes on, or a native library that it loads. A NAMESPACE option gives the required package a name that can qualify the classes and routines it supplies. This page specifies the directive, what a required package makes visible, the faults that requiring can raise and the two options. How a name is searched for as a file or as a library is the subject of the environment chapter, and the examples here name files that the program writes into the current directory.

Requiring a package

[dir.requires.create]

The operand of ::REQUIRES is a symbol or a string that names the package, and the names rule gives the spelling of each. Which of the two finds a file is a property of the file system, so that a name that has lower-case letters is best written as a string. The interpreter installs the required package as installation describes, which includes running its prolog, before the requiring package creates a class or runs its own prolog. An exit or return in the required prolog ends only that prolog, and the requiring package goes on. A directive with no operand, or with an operand that is neither a symbol nor a string, raises SYNTAX 19.904, found when the program is read. A name that finds no file raises 43.901 when the package is installed. The directive takes no code, and any clause after it that is not a null clause raises SYNTAX 99.916 when the program is read.

f = 'SPEC_DIR_REQUIRES_SYM.TMP'
call sysfiledelete f
call lineout f, 'say "lib prolog"'
call lineout f, 'exit'
call lineout f, '::routine from_lib public'
call lineout f, '  return "from lib"'
call lineout f
src = .array~of('say "prolog"', 'say from_lib()', -
  '::requires spec_dir_requires_sym.tmp')
p = .package~new('spec-dir-requires-sym', src)
src = .array~of('say "prolog 2"', '::requires "'f'"')
p = .package~new('spec-dir-requires-str', src)
call try '::requires'
call try '::requires ("'f'")'
call try '::requires 1'
call try '::requires "'f'" -- a comment', '', '/* more */', '::requires "'f'"'
call try '::requires "'f'"', 'say 1'
call sysfiledelete f
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  src = .array~new
  do i = 1 to arg()
    src~append(arg(i))
  end
  p = .package~new('spec-dir-requires-op', src)
  say arg(1) '=> ok'
  return
e: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

prolog

prolog 2
::requires => 19.904
::requires ("SPEC_DIR_REQUIRES_SYM.TMP") => 19.904
::requires 1 => 43.901
::requires "SPEC_DIR_REQUIRES_SYM.TMP" -- a comment => ok
::requires "SPEC_DIR_REQUIRES_SYM.TMP" => 99.916
[dir.requires.once]

A package that is required again is not installed again and its prolog does not run again. The requirement may come from the same package, from another package that requires it, or from a package that a required package requires, and the name may differ as long as it finds the same file. Every requirer sees the one package, so that the order in which a package is first required fixes the order of the prologs.

fa = 'spec-dir-requires-a.tmp'
fb = 'spec-dir-requires-b.tmp'
call sysfiledelete fa
call sysfiledelete fb
call lineout fa, 'say "a prolog"'
call lineout fa
call lineout fb, 'say "b prolog"'
call lineout fb, '::requires "'fa'"'
call lineout fb
src = .array~of('say "prolog"', -
  '::requires "'fb'"', -
  '::requires "'fa'"', -
  '::requires "./'fa'"', -
  '::requires "'fb'"')
p = .package~new('spec-dir-requires-once', src)
call sysfiledelete fa
call sysfiledelete fb

b prolog
prolog

What becomes visible

[dir.requires.visible]

A required package makes visible to the requiring package its public classes, which the class rule describes, and its public routines, which the routine rule describes. Its private classes and routines, and the variables that its prolog set, are not visible. Those two rules also give the order in which names are looked up among the package's own and the required ones.

f = 'spec-dir-requires-vis.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call lineout f, 'secret = "set in the lib prolog"'
call lineout f, '::class shown public'
call lineout f, '::class hidden'
call lineout f, '::routine open public'
call lineout f, '  return "open"'
call lineout f, '::routine closed'
call lineout f, '  return "closed"'
call lineout f
src = .array~of('say .shown~id', -
  'say .hidden', -
  'say open()', -
  'say symbol("secret")', -
  'signal on syntax name e', -
  'say closed()', -
  'e: say condition("o")~code', -
  '::requires "'f'"')
p = .package~new('spec-dir-requires-vis', src)
call sysfiledelete f

Faults

[dir.requires.failure]

A fault in requiring raises a SYNTAX condition in the requiring package, and the installation stops as the failure rule says. A required program with a fault in its text raises that fault's error, a fault that its prolog raises is raised again in the requiring package with the same code, and a required package that requires an absent file raises 43.901. A package that requires itself, or that is required by a package that it requires, directly or through others, raises SYNTAX 98.952. The cycle is found before the prolog of any package in it runs.

f = 'spec-dir-requires-bad.tmp'
g = 'spec-dir-requires-deep.tmp'
tx = 'spec-dir-requires-text.tmp'
c1 = 'spec-dir-requires-cyc1.tmp'
c2 = 'spec-dir-requires-cyc2.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call sysfiledelete g
call sysfiledelete tx
call sysfiledelete c1
call sysfiledelete c2
call lineout f, 'say "bad prolog"'
call lineout f, 'x = 1 / 0'
call lineout f
call lineout tx, '::frob'
call lineout tx
call lineout g, '::requires "spec-dir-requires-nosuchfile-xyz.rex"'
call lineout g
call lineout c1, 'say "cyc1 prolog"'
call lineout c1, '::requires "'c2'"'
call lineout c1
call lineout c2, 'say "cyc2 prolog"'
call lineout c2, '::requires "'c1'"'
call lineout c2
call try '::requires "'f'"'
call try '::requires "'g'"'
call try '::requires "'tx'"'
call try 'say "main prolog"', '::requires "'c1'"'
call try '::class k', '::frob'
call sysfiledelete f
call sysfiledelete g
call sysfiledelete tx
call sysfiledelete c1
call sysfiledelete c2
exit

  return

Libraries

[dir.requires.library]

With LIBRARY the operand names a native library, which the interpreter loads instead of a Rexx program, and a library that cannot be loaded raises SYNTAX 98.903. A package processes its LIBRARY directives first, wherever they stand in its text, and only then its other ::REQUIRES directives, so a library that cannot be loaded raises before any required program has run its prolog. A library can be required more than once. Whether a library name is case sensitive, and where libraries are searched for, are not specified here. The LIBRARY option does not combine with NAMESPACE: the two together raise SYNTAX 25.904.

f = 'rq-p.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call lineout f, 'say "required prolog"'
call lineout f
call try '::requires "rexxutil" library'
call try '::requires "rexxutil" library', '::requires "rexxutil" LIBRARY'
call try '::requires "'f'"', '::requires "spec_no_such_lib_xyz" library'
call try '::requires "spec_no_such_lib_xyz" library', '::requires "'f'"'
call try '::requires "rexxutil" library namespace a'
call try '::requires "rexxutil" namespace a library'
call sysfiledelete f
exit

  signal on syntax name e
  src = .array~new
  do i = 1 to arg()
    src~append(arg(i))
  end
  p = .package~new('spec-dir-requires-lib', src)
  say src~makestring('l', ' / ') '=> ok'
  return
e: say src~makestring('l', ' / ') '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

Namespaces

[dir.requires.namespace]

NAMESPACE takes a symbol, which becomes a name of the required package. A class or a routine that the package makes visible is then found by the name qualified with the namespace and a colon: ns:name(...) calls the routine and ns:name is the class, as in ns:name~new. Qualified names are symbols, so the namespace is matched without regard to case. The unqualified name is looked up as the routine rule and the class rule say. When two directives give one namespace name, the later one names its package. A string, or no symbol after NAMESPACE, raises SYNTAX 20.920, and a keyword other than LIBRARY or NAMESPACE, a repeated keyword or any further word raises 25.904, found when the program is read. The namespace name REXX belongs to the interpreter and raises 99.944.

fa = 'spec-dir-requires-nsa.tmp'
fb = 'spec-dir-requires-nsb.tmp'
call sysfiledelete fa
call sysfiledelete fb
call lineout fa, '::routine hello public'
call lineout fa, '  return "hello A"'
call lineout fa, '::class widget public'
call lineout fa, '::method who'
call lineout fa, '  return "widget A"'
call lineout fa
call lineout fb, '::routine hello public'
call lineout fb, '  return "hello B"'
call lineout fb, '::class widget public'
call lineout fb, '::method who'
call lineout fb, '  return "widget B"'
call lineout fb
src = .array~of('say hello()', -
  'say a:hello() b:hello() A:Hello()', -
  'say .widget~new~who a:widget~new~who b:widget~new~who', -
  '::requires "'fa'" namespace a', -
  '::requires "'fb'" namespace b')
p = .package~new('spec-dir-requires-ns', src)
src = .array~of('say hello() a:hello()', '::requires "'fb'"', -
  '::requires "'fa'" namespace a')
p = .package~new('spec-dir-requires-ns2', src)
src = .array~of('say a:hello()', '::requires "'fa'" namespace a', -
  '::requires "'fb'" namespace a')
p = .package~new('spec-dir-requires-ns3', src)
call try '::requires "'fa'" namespace'
call try '::requires "'fa'" namespace "a"'
call try '::requires "'fa'" namespace a b'
call try '::requires "'fa'" namespace a namespace b'
call try '::requires "'fa'" frob'
call try '::requires "'fa'" namespace rexx'
call try '::requires "'fa'" Namespace a'
call sysfiledelete fa
call sysfiledelete fb
exit

  say arg(1) '=> ok'
  return

[dir.requires.namespace.lookup]

A qualified name whose namespace no ::REQUIRES gave raises SYNTAX 98.987, and so does a qualified call of it. A qualified class that the namespace's package does not make visible raises 98.988, and a qualified routine that it does not make visible raises 43.902. What a package makes visible is what the visibility rule says, including the public classes and routines that it found through its own ::REQUIRES. A qualified name written as a function call needs the parenthesis to follow the name at once, and without it the name is read as a class. The CALL instruction does not accept the qualified form, as its error rule says.

fa = 'spec-dir-requires-lk.tmp'

call lineout fa, '::routine only_a public'

  'call try "say n:only_a()"', -
  'exit', -
  'try:', -

  '  interpret arg(1)', -
  '  return', -

  '::requires "'fc'" namespace n')

::OPTIONS

::OPTIONS option ...

rexxref: Directives > ::OPTIONS

Deviations: D103

::OPTIONS sets the defaults that the code of its package starts with. The defaults are the three NUMERIC settings, the TRACE setting, whether a routine takes the NUMERIC settings of its caller, the way that six conditions are raised, and whether the prolog runs when another package requires this one. The settings themselves are specified with NUMERIC and TRACE, and the conditions with their own pages in the conditions chapter. This page specifies the form of the directive, what each option sets, and how far it reaches.

The directive

[dir.options.syntax]

The words after ::OPTIONS are options. An option is a keyword, in any case, followed by its value, except PROLOG and NOPROLOG, which stand alone. Any number of options may be written in any order, on one directive or on several. When an option of one kind occurs twice, in one directive or in two, the one that stands later in the text wins, and options of different kinds all stay in force. A directive with no option does nothing. A word that is no keyword of an option, which a second value after a keyword also is, raises SYNTAX 25.924. The directive takes no code of its own: a clause after it that is not a null clause raises SYNTAX 99.916, as the section rule says. The faults are found when the program is read, so as the read rule says a program file with one writes nothing and exits with 256 minus the error number, 231 for 25.924.

src = .array~of('say digits() fuzz() form()', -
  '::options digits 23 form engineering', -
  '::options fuzz 3 digits 15', -
  '::OPTIONS Digits 11')
p = .package~new('spec-dir-options-syntax', src)
src = .array~of('say digits() fuzz() form()', '::options', '::options ;')
p = .package~new('spec-dir-options-syntax2', src)
call try '::options bogus'
call try '::options 5'
call try '::options "digits" 5'
call try '::options digits 5 6'
call try '::options form engineering digits 5'
call try '::options prolog 5'
call try '::options digits 5', 'say 1'
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  src = .array~new
  do i = 1 to arg()
    src~append(arg(i))
  end
  p = .package~new('spec-dir-options-try', src)
  say src~makestring('l', ' / ') '=> ok'
  return
e: say src~makestring('l', ' / ') '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

11 3 ENGINEERING
9 0 SCIENTIFIC
::options bogus => 25.924
::options 5 => 25.924
::options "digits" 5 => 25.924
::options digits 5 6 => 25.924
::options form engineering digits 5 => ok
::options prolog 5 => 25.924
::options digits 5 / say 1 => 99.916

say 'before'
::options bogus
[dir.options.scope]

The options of a package are the starting values of all its code. They reach the prolog, every ::ROUTINE and every method of the package, wherever the directive stands in the file, so that code written before the directive has them too. The NUMERIC and TRACE settings that they give are the defaults of the package that DIGITS, FUZZ and FORM name: a NUMERIC instruction without a value returns the setting to them. A NUMERIC or TRACE instruction changes only the setting of the code that runs it, as the scope rule says, and the next routine or method that starts is not affected. An internal routine and the text of an INTERPRET take the setting of the code that runs them, as the scope rules of the settings say, and not the option. The instruction TRACE with no value sets N, not the option, as the bare form says.

say 'prolog' digits() fuzz() form() trace()
call internal
say 'routine' r()
say 'method' .box~new~m()
numeric digits 20
numeric fuzz 3
numeric form scientific
trace n
say 'changed' digits() fuzz() form() trace()
call internal
say 'routine' r()
numeric digits
numeric fuzz
numeric form
trace
say 'reset' digits() fuzz() form() trace()
interpret 'say "interpret" digits()'
exit
internal: say 'internal' digits() fuzz() form() trace(); return
::options digits 12 fuzz 2 form engineering trace o
::routine r
  return digits() fuzz() form() trace()
::class box
::method m
  return digits() fuzz() form() trace()

prolog 12 2 ENGINEERING O
internal 12 2 ENGINEERING O
routine 12 2 ENGINEERING O
method 12 2 ENGINEERING O
changed 20 3 SCIENTIFIC N
internal 20 3 SCIENTIFIC N
routine 12 2 ENGINEERING O
reset 12 2 ENGINEERING N
interpret 12
[dir.options.package]

The options of a package belong to the code that is written in it. They do not reach the code of a package that this one requires, and the options of a required package do not reach the code that requires it. A routine of one package that another package calls starts with the options of the package that holds the routine, as the scope rule says for the NUMERIC settings.

f = 'spec-dir-options-lib.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call lineout f, '::options digits 15 fuzz 3 form engineering'
call lineout f, '::routine libr public'
call lineout f, '  return digits() fuzz() form()'
call lineout f
src = .array~of('say "main" digits() fuzz() form()', -
  'say "lib" libr()', -
  '::requires "'f'"', -
  '::options digits 6')
p = .package~new('spec-dir-options-main', src)
call sysfiledelete f

main 6 0 SCIENTIFIC
lib 15 3 ENGINEERING

The numeric options

[dir.options.numeric]

DIGITS, FUZZ and FORM set the NUMERIC settings that the code of the package starts with. DIGITS and FUZZ take a symbol or a string that the NUMERIC instruction would accept as its value, so that "7", 05, 1e2 and 5.0 are whole numbers. A value that is not a whole number of at least 1 raises SYNTAX 26.5 for DIGITS, and one that is not a whole number of at least 0 raises 26.6 for FUZZ. A symbol is never looked up as a variable. A missing value, or one that is not a symbol or a string, such as a sign or parentheses, raises 19.917 for DIGITS and 19.918 for FUZZ. FORM takes the symbol SCIENTIFIC or ENGINEERING in any case, and no abbreviation. A missing value or a string raises SYNTAX 20.925, and any other symbol 25.11. The faults are found when the program is read.

call try '::options digits "7" fuzz 05'
call try '::options digits 1e2'
call try '::options digits 5.0'
call try '::options digits abc'
call try '::options digits 1.5'
call try '::options digits 0'
call try '::options digits -1'
call try '::options digits (5)'
call try '::options digits'
call try '::options fuzz abc'
call try '::options fuzz -1'
call try '::options fuzz'
call try '::options form Engineering'
call try '::options form sci'
call try '::options form "scientific"'
call try '::options form'
exit

  p = .package~new('spec-dir-options-num', src)
  say arg(1) '=> ok'
  return
e: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

[dir.options.fuzz]

The two settings must stay apart: after each DIGITS or FUZZ is processed, DIGITS must exceed FUZZ, or the directive raises SYNTAX 33.1, as the fuzz rule says for the instruction. The check is made on the value that the other setting holds at that point, which is its default of 9 or 0 until an option sets it, and it is made after every option, so the order of the options matters. The error is found when the program is read.

call try '::options fuzz 8'
call try '::options fuzz 9'
call try '::options digits 4'
call try '::options digits 5 fuzz 5'
call try '::options digits 5 fuzz 4'
call try '::options fuzz 8 digits 10'
call try '::options digits 10 fuzz 8 digits 8'
call try '::options digits 10 fuzz 8', '::options digits 7'
call try '::options digits 24', '::options fuzz 21', '::options digits 21'
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  src = .array~of('say digits() fuzz()')
  text = arg(1)
  src~append(arg(1))
  do i = 2 to arg()
    src~append(arg(i))
    text = text '/' arg(i)
  end
  p = .package~new('spec-dir-options-fuzz', src)
  say text '=> ok'
  return
e: say text '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

[dir.options.inherit]

NUMERIC INHERIT makes a routine or a method of the package start with the three NUMERIC settings of the code that calls it, and NUMERIC NOINHERIT, which is the default, makes it start with the options and defaults of its own package. The word after NUMERIC must be INHERIT or NOINHERIT, and the last of the two in text order is used. A missing word, or a string, raises SYNTAX 20.935, and any other symbol 25.935, found when the program is read. With INHERIT the settings that DIGITS, FUZZ and FORM give still start the prolog, but a ::ROUTINE or a method does not use them. A routine of a package with INHERIT that a caller from another package calls takes the settings of that caller.

say 'start' digits()

numeric fuzz 1
numeric form engineering
say 'main' digits() fuzz() form()
say 'routine' r()
say 'method' .box~new~m()

call try '::options numeric 5'
exit

The trace option

[dir.options.trace]

TRACE sets the tracing setting that the prolog, every routine and every method of the package start with. Its value is a word that the TRACE instruction accepts, chosen by its first letter, so that Off and O are alike, and a letter that is not valid raises SYNTAX 24.1, which a string with a blank before the letter does too. A missing value, a sign and a parenthesis raise 19.919. The empty string is accepted and starts the code with N. The directive is stricter than the instruction in one respect: a number is not a setting and raises 24.1. The setting is what TRACE() returns when the code starts, and a TRACE instruction changes it for the running code only, as the scope rule says. A question mark before the letter is accepted, and what interactive tracing does belongs to the TRACE instruction. What TRACE() returns when the code starts after a question mark with no letter after it is ?N, as the Deviation states.

call try 'o'
call try 'Off'
call try 'normal'
call try 'N'
call try '"n"'
call try 'x'
call try '3'
call try '""'
call try '-1'
call try '+'
call try '(n)'
call try '" n"'
call try ''
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  src = .array~of('say "start" trace()', 'trace n', -
    'say "changed" trace() .box~new~m r()', -
    '::options trace' arg(1), -
    '::routine r', '  return trace()', -
    '::class box', '::method m', '  return trace()')
  p = .package~new('spec-dir-options-trace', src)
  return
e: say 'trace' arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

changed N O O
start O
changed N O O
start N
changed N N N
start N
changed N N N
start N
changed N N N

trace 3 => 24.1
start N
changed N N N

trace + => 19.919
trace (n) => 19.919
trace " n" => 24.1
trace  => 19.919

The condition options

[dir.options.condition]

ERROR, FAILURE, LOSTDIGITS, NOSTRING, NOTREADY and NOVALUE each take the value SYNTAX or CONDITION. CONDITION is the default and leaves the condition as the conditions chapter specifies it. SYNTAX makes the condition that no trap answers raise a SYNTAX condition instead, with these codes: 98.970 for ERROR, 98.971 for FAILURE, 98.972 for LOSTDIGITS, 98.973 for NOSTRING, 98.974 for NOTREADY and 98.986 for NOVALUE. The clause that raised it ends there as the SYNTAX rule says, and RC is 98 in the trap that catches it. Without a trap the program ends as the rule for an untrapped SYNTAX says, with exit status 158. A FAILURE raised as SYNTAX is not passed on to the ERROR trap, as the second example shows. A FAILURE that no trap answers, which the untrapped rule would ignore, is answered as ERROR here, so with ERROR SYNTAX it raises 98.970 when FAILURE is left at CONDITION, as the third example shows. A missing value or a string raises SYNTAX 20.929 and any other symbol 25.927, both when the program is read.

call try 'error'
call try 'failure'
call try 'lostdigits'
call try 'nostring'
call try 'notready'
call try 'novalue'
exit
try:
  which = arg(1)
  signal on syntax name e
  select
    when which = 'error' then address system 'exit 3'
    when which = 'failure' then address nosuchenv 'echo x'
    when which = 'lostdigits' then do; numeric digits 3; say 12345 + 0; end
    when which = 'nostring' then say 'a' || .nstr~new
    when which = 'notready' then say linein('nosuchfile.zzz')
    when which = 'novalue' then say undefinedvar
  end
  say which 'went on'
  return
e: say which condition('o')~code rc
  return
::class nstr
::method string
  return .nil

[dir.options.condition.trap]

A trap still answers the condition with its own name: with SIGNAL ON, CALL ON or the ANY trap on, the condition is raised as ERROR, FAILURE, LOSTDIGITS, NOSTRING, NOTREADY or NOVALUE and not as SYNTAX, and the answering trap is the one that the choice rule picks. The option applies only while the trap instructions have left the condition alone: a SIGNAL or CALL instruction that turns the trap of the condition ON or OFF, or the trap of ANY, ends the option for that condition for the rest of the routine or method in which it ran, so that an OFF condition is ignored again. A CALL instruction does so for ERROR, FAILURE and NOTREADY, the conditions of the option that CALL can trap, and CALL ON or OFF of ANY does so for these three only: for LOSTDIGITS, NOSTRING and NOVALUE the option stays in force. An internal routine takes this state from its caller, and the instructions that it runs end the option for its own code only, so that its caller still has the state it had when the routine returns. A SIGNAL or CALL in the text of an INTERPRET ends the option for the code that runs the INTERPRET. A ::ROUTINE and a method start without the state, and the option applies there afresh. A SYNTAX condition that the option raises is an ordinary one, which SIGNAL ON SYNTAX answers.

call try 1
call try 2
call try 3
call try 4
call try 5
call try 6
call try 7
call try 8
call try 9
call try 10
call try 11
call try 12
call try 13
call try 14
call try 15
exit
try:
  which = arg(1)
  signal on syntax name e
  select
    when which = 1 then say 'one' unset1
    when which = 2 then do; signal on novalue name t; say 'two' unset2; end
    when which = 3 then do; signal off novalue; say 'three' unset3; end
    when which = 4 then do; signal on any name t; say 'four' unset4; end
    when which = 5 then do; signal off any; say 'five' unset5; end
    when which = 6 then do
      call on error name tc; address system 'exit 3'
    end
    when which = 7 then do; call off error; address system 'exit 3'; end
    when which = 8 then call inner
    when which = 9 then do; signal off novalue; call inner; end
    when which = 10 then do; signal off novalue; call routine10; end
    when which = 11 then do; call off any; say 'eleven' unset11; end
    when which = 12 then do; call off any; address system 'exit 3'; end
    when which = 13 then do; call inner13; say 'thirteen' unset13; end
    when which = 14 then do
      interpret 'signal off novalue'
      say 'fourteen' unset14
    end
    when which = 15 then do
      signal on any name t
      numeric digits 3
      say 12345 + 0
    end
  end
  say which 'went on'
  return
t: say which 'trap' condition('c')
  return
tc: say which 'call trap' condition('c')
  return
e: say which 'syntax' condition('o')~code
  return
inner: say 'inner' unset8
  return
inner13: signal off novalue
  return

[dir.options.condition.all]

ALL is a single option that gives its value, SYNTAX or CONDITION, to each of the six. It is processed in text order like any option, so an option that follows it overrides its value for one condition, and one that precedes it is overridden. A missing value or a string after ALL raises SYNTAX 20.929, and any other symbol 25.927.

call try 'error'
call try 'novalue'
call try 'lostdigits'
call try 'nothing'
exit
try:
  which = arg(1)
  signal on syntax name e
  select
    when which = 'error' then address system 'exit 3'
    when which = 'novalue' then say undefinedvar
    when which = 'lostdigits' then do; numeric digits 3; say 12345 + 0; end
    otherwise nop
  end
  say which 'went on'
  return
e: say which condition('o')~code
  return

The prolog option

[dir.options.prolog]

PROLOG and NOPROLOG decide what a ::REQUIRES of the package does with its prolog: with PROLOG, the default, the prolog runs, and with NOPROLOG it is skipped, so that a package of routines and classes can be required without its start-up code. The last of the two in text order is used. The installation of the package is not affected, so its routines and classes exist all the same. The program that was started runs its prolog whatever the option says. Loading the text of a package with the Package class follows the same rule as a requirement, as the first example shows. The option acts on a package that is required or loaded as a package only: a file that a program calls as an external routine runs its code from the start, whatever the option says, as the third example shows.

f = 'spec-dir-options-pro1.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call lineout f, 'say "prolog of one"'
call lineout f, '::options noprolog'
call lineout f, '::routine one public'
call lineout f, '  return "one"'
call lineout f, '::class kone public'
call lineout f, '::method activate class'
call lineout f, '  say "activate kone"'
call lineout f
g = 'spec-dir-options-pro2.tmp'
call sysfiledelete g
call lineout g, 'say "prolog of two"'
call lineout g, '::options noprolog prolog'
call lineout g, '::routine two public'
call lineout g, '  return "two"'
call lineout g
src = .array~of('say "main prolog"', 'say one() two() .kone~id', -
  '::requires "'f'"', '::requires "'g'"')
p = .package~new('spec-dir-options-main3', src)
src = .array~of('say "never written"', '::options noprolog')
p = .package~new('spec-dir-options-main4', src)
call sysfiledelete f
call sysfiledelete g

activate kone
prolog of two
main prolog
one two KONE

say 'this prolog runs'
::options noprolog

this prolog runs

f = 'spec-dir-options-pro3.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call lineout f, 'say "prolog of the file" arg(1)'
call lineout f, 'return "answer"'
call lineout f, '::options noprolog'
call lineout f
call (f) 'x'
say 'result' result
call (f) 'y'
call sysfiledelete f

prolog of the file x
result answer
prolog of the file y

Deviations

[dir.options.deviation.103]

Under ::OPTIONS TRACE ?, the TRACE builtin answers ?N when the code starts, as after the instruction trace ? at the start of a program: the question mark turns interactive tracing on and the letter stays N, the default. ooRexx answers the null string.

say trace()
::options trace ?

?N

::RESOURCE

::RESOURCE name [END delimiter]

rexxref: Directives > ::RESOURCE

::RESOURCE puts lines of text into a package. The lines are not code: the interpreter does not read them as clauses, and a program reads them back as data by the name of the resource. A resource is the way to carry a template, a table or a message text inside the file of a program. This page specifies the directive and where the data ends, the lines as they are kept, and the way that a program reaches them. The methods of the collection that holds the resources belong to the classes chapter, and the examples use only those that are needed to read an item.

The directive

[dir.resource.create]

The directive clause names the resource, and the lines that follow it are its data, up to a line that starts with the end delimiter. The name is a symbol or a string. The delimiter follows the word END, in any case, and is a symbol or a string too. Without END the delimiter is ::END. A delimiter that is a symbol is taken in upper case, and one that is a string as written, so that end done stands for the text DONE and end "done" for done. The match is case sensitive and is made at the start of the line: a line ends the data when its first characters are the delimiter, wherever the line goes on after them, and a line that has the delimiter after a blank, or in another case, is data. The delimiter line is not part of the data, and the clause that follows it is the first clause after the resource. A semicolon after the directive ends the directive clause, and what follows it on that line is dropped and never becomes a clause. A comment may follow the directive.

a = .resources~tune
say a~items
do line over a
  say '['line']'
end
say .resources~dflt~items .resources~sym~items .resources~str~items -
  .resources~semi~items
::resource tune end "="
Hold the line
=====
::resource dflt
line one
 ::END indented is data
::end lowercase is data
::END text after the delimiter is ignored
::resource sym end STOPHERE
a
Stophere is data
STOPHEREX is the delimiter line
::resource str end "end of it" -- a comment
x
end of it
::resource semi end "e"; ignored text
body
e

1
[Hold the line]
3 2 1 1
[dir.resource.name]

The name that a program reads a resource by is the name in upper case, whether it was written as a symbol or as a string, so ::resource "Mixed" is read as MIXED. Names are not otherwise changed: a name that is a string may hold blanks. A package holds one resource of a name, and a second ::RESOURCE of a name that is the same in upper case, whatever its spelling, raises SYNTAX 99.942. A resource may have the same name as a class, a method or a routine. A directive whose name is missing, or is neither a symbol nor a string, raises 19.920. The errors are found when the program is read.

say .resources~allindexes~sort~makestring('l', ',')
say .resources['MIXED']~items .resources['A B']~items
say .resources['Mixed']
exit
::resource "Mixed" end "x"
one
x
::resource "a b"
::END
::resource 12
::END
::resource box
::END
::class box
::routine box
  return 1

[dir.resource.delimiter]

A word after the name that is not END raises SYNTAX 25.926, and so does LIBRARY. END with no delimiter after it, or with a delimiter that is neither a symbol nor a string, such as a number sign or a parenthesis, raises 19.921. A token after the delimiter, other than a semicolon, a comment or the end of the line, raises 21.914. A string delimiter that is empty is a prefix of every line and so ends the data at the first line: the resource is empty. The data must end: when no line starts with the delimiter, the directive raises SYNTAX 99.943, so that a delimiter written as a symbol cannot end the data with a line in lower case. All of these faults are found when the program is read.

call try '::resource a bogus', 'x', '::END'
call try '::resource a library', 'x', '::END'
call try '::resource a end', 'x'
call try '::resource a end +', 'x'
call try '::resource a end ("q")', 'x', 'q'
call try '::resource a end "q" junk', 'x', 'q'
call try '::resource a end "q" ,', 'x', 'q'
call try '::resource a end "q"', 'x'
call try '::resource a end q', 'x', 'q'
call try '::resource a end q', 'x', 'Q'
call try '::resource a', 'x'
call try '::resource a', 'x', '::end'
call try '::resource a end ""', 'x', '::class k'
call try '::resource a end 5', 'x', '5 is a number'

[dir.resource.section]

A resource has no section of code of its own. The clauses after the delimiter line that are not null clauses belong to no directive, and one raises SYNTAX 99.916, as the section rule says. A line of the data that starts with two colons is data, and so is every other line: the data is not checked in any way, so that it may hold unbalanced quotes, comment starts and directives. The next directive may follow the delimiter line at once. A resource inside a class section does not end the class: the methods that follow it belong to the class as before.

call try '::resource a', '::END', 'say 1'
call try '::resource a', '::END', '', '-- a comment', '::class k'
call try '::resource a', ' say "unbalanced', '::method m', '::END'
call try '::class k', '::resource a', 'x', '::END', '::method m', ' return 1'
exit

The data

[dir.resource.lines]

The data of a resource is the list of its lines, in order, each as written in the file: leading and trailing blanks, tabs and empty lines are kept, and the line end is not part of a line. A line end of one carriage return and a line feed ends the line like a line feed alone. A resource with no line between the directive and the delimiter has no items, and neither has one whose delimiter is the empty string, since the first line is then the delimiter line. The lines are not read for comments, strings or symbols, so that a line holds exactly its characters.

do name over 'BLANK', 'TAIL', 'EMPTY', 'GONE', 'MIXED'
  a = .resources[name]
  say name a~items
  do i = 1 to a~items
    say '  ['a[i]']' a[i]~length
  end
end

::END
::resource tail
x  
y	
::END
::resource empty
::END
::resource gone end ""
this line is the delimiter line
::resource mixed
/* not a comment */ "not a string" -- not a comment
::END

  [ ] 1
  [  ] 2
  [] 0
TAIL 2
  [x  ] 3
  [y	] 2
EMPTY 0
GONE 0
MIXED 1
  [/* not a comment */ "not a string" -- not a comment] 51

Reaching the data

[dir.resource.access]

The environment symbol .RESOURCES holds the resources of the package whose code reads it. It is a collection indexed by the resource names in upper case, and each item is an array of the lines of that resource. It is there from the start of the prolog, and in every routine and method of the package. A package with no ::RESOURCE has no .RESOURCES, and the symbol has its own text as value. The index is looked up exactly, so that .resources['COBALT'] finds the resource named cobalt and .resources['cobalt'] finds nothing. The collection is each package's own: the resources of a required package are not in the .RESOURCES of the package that requires it, and the other way round, so that a routine of the required package reads its own. The arrays are shared by all code of the package: an item that one routine changes, or an array that it extends, is changed for every later read, in any routine or method of the package.

say 'none:' .resources
say .box~new~m
say r()

call sysfiledelete f
call lineout f, '::routine libres public'
call lineout f, '  return .resources~items .resources~allindexes'
call lineout f, '::resource inlib'
call lineout f, 'x'
call lineout f, '::END'
call lineout f
src = .array~of('say "lib:" libres()', 'say "main:" .resources~items', -
  'say "second:" later()', '::requires "'f'"', -
  '::resource inmain', 'y', '::END', '::resource second', '::END', -
  '::routine later public', '  return .resources~items')
p = .package~new('spec-dir-resource-main', src)
call sysfiledelete f
::class box
::method m
  return .resources
::routine r
  return .resources

::ANNOTATE

::ANNOTATE PACKAGE | CLASS name | METHOD name | ATTRIBUTE name | CONSTANT name | ROUTINE name {annotation value}...

rexxref: Directives > ::ANNOTATE

::ANNOTATE attaches notes to the parts of a package. A note is an annotation, a name with a text as its value, and a program that holds the object of a package, class, method or routine can read the annotations that were declared for it. The interpreter does nothing with them: no annotation name has a meaning of its own, so they carry information for tools and for the program itself. This page specifies what the directive may name, the form of the names and values, and which annotations a program finds. The methods that read and change annotations belong to the classes chapter, and the examples use only ANNOTATION and ANNOTATIONS, and the methods that reach an object.

The form

[dir.annotate.syntax]

After the directive word comes a kind word, in any case: PACKAGE, CLASS, METHOD, ATTRIBUTE, CONSTANT or ROUTINE. Every kind but PACKAGE then has a target name, a symbol or a string, and the rest of the clause is a list of annotations, each a name and a value. The list may be empty. A missing kind raises SYNTAX 20.924, a word that is no kind 25.928, and a missing target name 19.925. The directive takes no code: a clause after it that is not a null clause raises SYNTAX 99.916, as the section rule says, so that the directive ends the code of the method or routine before it. These faults are found when the program is read, so as the read rule says a program file with one writes nothing and exits with 256 minus the error number, 236 for 20.924.

call try '::annotate'
call try '::annotate frob x a b'
call try '::annotate class'
call try '::annotate package'
call try '::annotate package a b', '', '-- a comment', '::class k'
call try '::class k', '::annotate CLASS K a b; ::annotate class k c d'
call try '::class k', '::method m', '  return 1', '::annotate method m a b'
call try '::class k', '::method m', '::annotate method m a b', '  return 1'
exit

  say src~makestring('l', ' / ') '=> ok'
  return
e: say src~makestring('l', ' / ') '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

::annotate
[dir.annotate.value]

Each annotation is a name followed by a value. The name is a symbol, which is taken in upper case and never looked up as a variable. A name that is not a symbol, a string or an operator for instance, raises SYNTAX 20.919. The value is a string, a symbol or a number with an optional sign, and is kept as text: a string as written and a symbol in upper case, which includes a number that is written as a symbol such as 1e3. A sign before a number is kept and joined to it, also when a blank stands between them, and the number is kept as written. A symbol may hold periods, as .abc and a.b do. A value in parentheses raises 19.923, and so does a sign before anything but a number: before a sign, a string or a symbol that is no number. A list with an unpaired word raises 19.924. A name given twice, in one directive or in several, keeps the value that comes last in text order, and the other names are kept. The names and values do not depend on one another or on any variable of the program.

p = .context~package
a = p~annotations
do name over a~allindexes~sort
  say name '=' '['a[name]']'
end

What is annotated

[dir.annotate.target]

The target of a CLASS, ROUTINE, METHOD, ATTRIBUTE or CONSTANT annotation is an element that an earlier directive of the same package declared, found by its name with case ignored, whether the target was written as a symbol or as a string. A class or a routine is found among those declared before the directive, however many directives lie between. A method, an attribute or a constant is found only among those declared in the section of the most recent ::CLASS, or, before any class, among the methods that no class holds. A target that is not found, which includes one that is declared later, in another class, or by another package that was required or supplied by the interpreter, raises SYNTAX 99.945. The directive with no annotation is checked in the same way. The error is found when the program is read.

call try '::annotate class k a b'
call try '::annotate class k'
call try '::class k', '::annotate class k a b'

call try '::method m', '::annotate method m a b'
call try '::method m', '::class k', '::annotate method m a b'
exit

[dir.annotate.kind]

The kind word says which declarations the name is looked for in. CLASS finds a class, ROUTINE a routine and PACKAGE needs no name and annotates the package itself. METHOD finds a method that a ::METHOD declared, and also the method of an attribute or a constant, whose names are the attribute's name, with an equals sign for a setter, and the constant's name. ATTRIBUTE finds an attribute that ::ATTRIBUTE or the ATTRIBUTE option of ::METHOD declared and no other method, and the annotation is attached to both of the methods of the attribute that exist. CONSTANT finds a constant. An element is not found by the wrong kind word, and the error is SYNTAX 99.945. A name that holds an equals sign has to be written as a string. A method that was declared with the CLASS option, and an attribute that was, are found in the same way as the others. When a class has an instance method and a class method of one name, the annotation goes to the instance method, whichever of the two directives comes first, and the class method has none. A class method is annotated when no instance method has the name.

call try '::routine r', '::annotate package r a b'
exit

Reading the annotations

[dir.annotate.read]

The annotations of an element are kept with its object. The ANNOTATION message of the object of a package, class, method or routine, with an annotation name, returns the value as a string, or .nil when the element has no annotation of that name, and the name is looked up in upper case. The ANNOTATIONS message returns a table of all of them indexed by name. The annotation of an attribute is found on both of its methods, and that of a constant on the method of the constant. An annotation is not inherited: a class that names an annotated class as its superclass has none of its annotations, and the same name on a class and on its method are two separate annotations. A copy of an annotated routine or method keeps its annotations.

p = .context~package
say 'package' p~annotation('maint') p~annotations~items
say 'class' .k~annotation('X') .k~annotation('y') .k~annotations~items
say 'sub' .sub~annotations~items
m = .k~method('M')
say 'method' m~annotation('v') m~annotation('x') m~annotations~items
say 'copy' m~copy~annotation('V')
say 'attribute' .k~method('AT')~annotation('P') -
  .k~method('AT=')~annotation('P')
say 'constant' .k~method('C')~annotation('P')
r = p~findroutine('R')
say 'routine' r~annotation('p') r~copy~annotation('P') r~annotations~items
say 'none' (p~annotation('nothing') == .nil)

Conditions

ANSI: 8.2.1, 8.4.1; rexxref: Conditions and Condition Traps; Conditions and Condition Traps > Action Taken when a Condition Is Not Trapped

A condition is an event that a program can ask to be told about. The interpreter raises one when a command fails, when an unset variable is read, when an error is found in a running clause, when a stream cannot deliver, and when the program asks for one itself. What happens next depends on the trap for that condition: a program switches a trap on or off with the instructions SIGNAL and CALL, whose pages specify the syntax of those forms. This chapter specifies the conditions, what a trap does when its condition is raised, and what a program can learn about the condition afterwards.

The pages of this chapter are:

  • Condition traps: which trap answers a condition, what SIGNAL ON and CALL ON each do, the delayed state, and how far a trap reaches.
  • Condition information: the condition object, the variables RC and SIGL, and how an error reaches the caller of the code that raised it.
  • SYNTAX, ERROR and FAILURE, HALT, NOVALUE, NOSTRING, NOMETHOD, NOTREADY and LOSTDIGITS: one page for each condition, with when it is raised, what it carries and which traps answer it.
  • USER conditions: the conditions that a program names itself.
  • Error numbers: the numbers of the SYNTAX conditions and what each means.

The RAISE instruction, which raises a condition on purpose, has a page of its own among the instructions. The CONDITION builtin owns what a program reads back from a trapped condition, and this chapter links its rules.

The conditions

[cond.index.names]

The conditions are named ANY, ERROR, FAILURE, HALT, LOSTDIGITS, NOMETHOD, NOSTRING, NOTREADY, NOVALUE, SYNTAX and USER. A USER condition is the word USER with a name, and it is a condition of its own, whatever its name: user error is not ERROR, and an ERROR trap does not catch it. The form of the name and which of the two instructions accepts which condition are in the ON rule of SIGNAL and that of CALL. ANY is not raised by anything. It is a trap that catches the others, as the choice rule says.

call on user Foo name h1
call on user error name h2
call on any name h3
signal on error name er
call r1
call r2
call r3
exit
r1: raise user foo return
r2: raise user error return
r3: raise user baz return
h1: say 'h1' condition('c'); return
h2: say 'h2' condition('c'); return
h3: say 'h3' condition('c'); return
er: say 'ERROR trap'

h1 USER FOO
h2 USER ERROR
h3 USER BAZ

Trap states

[cond.index.state]

Every condition has a trap with one of three states: OFF, ON and DELAY. A program starts with every trap OFF, and the instructions SIGNAL ON, CALL ON, SIGNAL OFF and CALL OFF set the state of the trap of their condition, which is what the S option of CONDITION reads back. DELAY is the state of a CALL trap while its handler runs, and the delay rule specifies it. The state of each condition is its own, and the trap of ANY has a state of its own beside those of the conditions it catches. A condition whose trap is OFF, and which no ANY trap catches, is untrapped, and the untrapped rule says what then happens.

address system
x = undefinedvar
'exit 3'
say 'ignored' rc
signal on novalue name n
y = undefinedvar2
n: say 'trapped' condition('c') condition('s')
signal off novalue
z = undefinedvar3
say 'off again' condition('s')

ignored 3
trapped NOVALUE OFF
off again OFF

When nothing traps a condition

[cond.index.untrapped]

When a condition is raised and no trap answers it, as the choice rule decides, ERROR, FAILURE, LOSTDIGITS, NOSTRING, NOTREADY, NOVALUE and the user conditions are ignored: the clause goes on as if nothing had happened, and the trap stays OFF. The exceptions are the FAILURE of a command, which the fallback rule says the ERROR trap answers, and the six conditions that the package's ::OPTIONS makes a SYNTAX condition. HALT and NOMETHOD are not ignored. An untrapped HALT raises SYNTAX 4.1 instead, and an untrapped NOMETHOD SYNTAX 97.1, or SYNTAX 97.2 when the message went to a private method that its sender may not run, as the NOMETHOD rule says. That SYNTAX condition is raised at the same place, so a SYNTAX trap catches it with CONDITION('C') answering SYNTAX. An ANY trap catches HALT and NOMETHOD before they would become SYNTAX, so the program sees their own names then. SYNTAX itself is not ignored, and the next rule says what it does.

address system
numeric digits 3
'exit 3'
address nosuch
'exit 3'
x = 12345 + 1
y = 'a' || .nostr~new
z = nosuchvar
w = linein()
call r
say 'ignored' x '['w']'
signal on syntax name s1
call rh
s1: say condition('c') condition('o')~code rc
signal on syntax name s2
x = .nil~nosuchmethod
s2: say condition('c') condition('o')~code rc
signal on any name a
call rh
a: say condition('c')
signal on any name b
x = .nil~nosuchmethod
b: say condition('c')
exit
r: raise user foo return
rh: raise halt return

[cond.index.syntax]

A SYNTAX condition that no trap catches ends the clause in which it was raised, and then every clause that is running a call, a function or a message at that moment, back to the main program, as the propagation rule says. The program then ends. It writes a report of the error to its standard error stream, whose text is not specified, and its exit code is 256 minus the number of the error, so that the error 97.1 gives 159 and 42.3 gives 214. The output that the clauses before the error wrote stays written. The subcode does not enter the exit code.

x = .nil~nosuchmethod
say 'not reached'

say 'before'
call mid
say 'not reached'
exit
mid:
  say 'in mid'
  x = 1 % 0
  say 'not reached in mid'

in mid
[cond.index.read]

An error that is found while a program is read, before any of its clauses runs, is not a condition that a trap can see, except in the text of an INTERPRET instruction, where the same fault is an ordinary SYNTAX condition. The reading rule of the lexical chapter lists those errors and gives the exit code.

SYNTAX 13.1

Condition traps

ANSI: 8.2.4, 8.4.1; rexxref: Conditions and Condition Traps > Action Taken when a Condition Is Trapped

Deviations: D64, D75, D104

A trap is the setting that tells the interpreter what to do when a condition is raised, and there is one for each condition. A SIGNAL trap moves control to a label as SIGNAL does and abandons the clause that raised the condition. A CALL trap lets the clause finish and then calls a routine, which returns to the clause after it. This page specifies which trap answers a condition, what each kind of trap does, the state that keeps a CALL trap from calling itself, and the code that a trap reaches. What the program learns about the condition is on the information page, and the syntax that sets a trap is on the pages of SIGNAL and CALL.

Which trap answers

[cond.traps.choice]

When a condition is raised, the trap of that condition answers it if its state is ON or DELAY. When it is OFF, the ANY trap answers instead if its state is ON or DELAY. When neither is on, the condition is untrapped, except that the FAILURE of a command then goes to the ERROR trap, as the fallback rule says. A trap that answers a condition changes only its own state, so every other trap, ANY included, stays as it was. The two kinds of trap are equal in this: a CALL trap for the condition wins over a SIGNAL trap for ANY, and a SIGNAL trap for the condition wins over a CALL trap for ANY. A condition that the ANY trap catches is still itself: CONDITION('C') answers its own name, and the default label or routine of an ANY trap is ANY. A condition whose own trap was switched off explicitly does not keep ANY from answering. A CALL trap for ANY answers only the conditions that CALL can trap, and a SIGNAL trap for ANY answers all of them. A user condition is answered by the trap of its own name, and the ANY trap catches the user conditions that have none.

call on any name a
call on user foo name f
signal on novalue name nv
call r1
call r2
call r3
x = undefinedvar
exit

r2: raise user bar return
r3: raise halt return
a: say 'a' condition('c'); return
f: say 'f' condition('c'); return
nv: say 'nv' condition('c')

[cond.traps.replace]

A trap has one setting at a time, and the latest SIGNAL ON, SIGNAL OFF, CALL ON or CALL OFF for its condition is that setting: the state, the kind (SIGNAL or CALL) and the name come from that instruction alone. A CALL ON and a SIGNAL ON for the same condition therefore do not coexist, whichever came first, and an ON with no NAME has the default name, not the name of an earlier ON. The traps of other conditions are not touched.

SIGNAL traps

[cond.traps.signal]

When a SIGNAL trap answers a condition, the clause that raised it ends at once, so that an assignment is not made, and a command whose string was being evaluated is not sent. A command whose return code raised ERROR or FAILURE has already run, and RC holds its return code. The state of the trap becomes OFF, the condition is recorded as the information page says, and control goes to the label of the trap as SIGNAL goes to a label, ending the open DO, LOOP, SELECT and IF constructs of the routine as that rule says. The label is the one that the NAME option gave, and the name of the condition when there was none. The trap is OFF at the label, so a second condition of the same kind that the code there raises is not trapped unless that code switches the trap on again or an ANY trap is ON, which the answer did not change.

do i = 1 to 3
  say 'loop' i
  if i = 2 then x = 1 + 'a'

exit

x = 1 + 'b'
say 'not reached either'

The label of a SIGNAL trap is looked for when the condition is raised, not when the trap is switched on. When there is no such label among the labels of the code that holds the trap, the trap, which is already OFF, raises SYNTAX 16.1 at the same clause, and a SYNTAX trap that is ON catches that error as any other. A routine or a method looks among its own labels, so a name that is a label of the main program only is no label there.

CALL traps

[cond.traps.call]

When a CALL trap answers a condition, the clause that raised it finishes first, so that a command has run and an assignment has been made. The state of the trap becomes DELAY, the condition is recorded, and a routine is called before the next clause starts. The next clause is the one after it in the same place, so the call is made inside a DO, a SELECT or an IF that holds the clause, and between the clauses of the text of an INTERPRET. When the clause that raised the condition ends the program, as an EXIT in the main program or the last clause does, the routine of the trap is called before the program ends. When it is the RETURN of a routine, the routine of the trap is called after the value of the RETURN is computed and before the caller goes on, and it sees the variables of the routine that returned. The caller then goes on with the clause after the CALL, or with the rest of the expression of the clause that invoked the routine as a function. What an EXIT inside an internal routine does with a pending CALL trap is a Deviation. The routine is the one that CALL finds for the name of the trap, which is the name of the condition when there was no NAME. It gets one argument, the condition object. The call does not change RESULT, and what the routine returns is dropped. When the routine returns, the trap is ON again, and the clause after the one that raised the condition runs. When the routine is an internal routine, SIGL is set as a CALL sets it, to the line of the clause that raised the condition, which for a RETURN or an EXIT is that clause itself and not the CALL. A routine without PROCEDURE shares the variables of the caller, RC among them. When the routine is a ::ROUTINE, a built-in function or an external routine, SIGL is not set, and it keeps the value it had.

    otherwise nop

  say 'in loop' rc
end
interpret "'exit 6'; say 'in text' rc; say 'text end'"
say 'after interpret'
exit
one: return 'kept'
h: say 'handler' arg() arg(1)~class condition('c') condition('i'),
    condition('s') rc sigl
  return 'dropped'

[cond.traps.call.state]

A handler that a CALL trap calls is a routine like any other, so the changes it makes to the states of the traps are undone when it returns: a CALL OFF in it does not leave the trap OFF, and a CALL ON with another name does not change the name. While it runs, the state of the trap that called it is DELAY, as CONDITION shows.

[cond.traps.call.label]

When the routine of a CALL trap is not found, the call is an ordinary CALL of a name that is no routine, and raises SYNTAX 43.1 after the clause that raised the condition has finished.

The delayed state

[cond.traps.delay]

While the state of a CALL trap is DELAY, a condition that is raised for it again does not call the routine. ERROR, FAILURE and NOTREADY raised again are ignored. Every other condition that is raised is held, and the held ones are answered in the order raised when the state of the trap changes. A CALL OFF or SIGNAL OFF for the condition drops them. A CALL ON or SIGNAL ON for the condition answers them at the end of that instruction, with the trap that the instruction set. When the routine returns, the CALL trap answers them by calling the routine again. A SIGNAL trap is never DELAY. The held conditions are Deviation 75.

address system
call on error name h
'exit 3'
say 'main' rc
exit
h: say 'enter h' rc
  'exit 4'
  say 'in h after' rc condition('s')
  return

enter h 3
in h after 4 DELAY
main 4

  say 'enter h' n condition('s')
  y = linein()

  return

Where a trap reaches

[cond.traps.scope]

The states of the traps belong to the code that runs, which is the main program, a routine, a method or an internal routine, and each starts with states of its own. An internal routine, which a CALL or a function call reaches by its label, starts with a copy of the states of its caller, names, kinds and DELAY included, and what it does to the copy is not seen by the caller after it returns. A ::ROUTINE, a method and a routine made from other source text start with every trap OFF. The text of an INTERPRET runs in the code that holds it and shares its states, so a trap that the text switches on stays on after it. Because an internal routine has a copy, a SIGNAL trap that answers a condition in it jumps to a label of the code that holds the routine, and a RETURN there returns from the routine, as the SIGNAL rule says.

Deviations

[cond.traps.deviation.64]

When the CALL that a CALL trap makes fails, and a SYNTAX trap is ON in the code that holds the CALL trap, that trap answers the SYNTAX condition at once, before the next clause runs, and SIGL is the line of the clause that raised the condition. The CALL fails when the routine is not found, which is SYNTAX 43.1, and when a SYNTAX error leaves the routine. In ooRexx the next clause runs first, and SIGL is its line.

Condition information

ANSI: 8.4.1, 9.5.3; rexxref: Conditions and Condition Traps > Condition Information; Conditions and Condition Traps > Condition Information > Condition Object

When a trap answers a condition, the interpreter records what it knows about the condition, and the code that the trap reaches can read it. The record holds the name of the condition, the kind of the trap, its state, a description, and an object that some conditions carry. It is read with the CONDITION builtin, which owns what each option answers, and as a condition object, a directory with one entry for each piece of information. The trap also sets the variables RC and SIGL, and an error that no trap in the code that raised it answers goes on to the code that called it. This page specifies the record, the condition object, the two variables and that journey, and the traps page specifies when a trap answers.

The record

[cond.information.record]

When a SIGNAL trap or a CALL trap answers a condition, the condition is recorded for the code that the trap reaches: the label's code for a SIGNAL trap, and the routine that a CALL trap calls. The record holds the name of the condition, the instruction of the trap, SIGNAL or CALL, the state of the trap, the description and the additional object, which CONDITION answers with its options. The scope rule of CONDITION also says which code holds a record and how long it stays. A condition that no trap answers records nothing: it is ignored, or it becomes a SYNTAX condition, as the untrapped rule says.

x = undefinedvar
'exit 3'
say '['condition('c')']' (condition('o') == .nil)

NOVALUE SIGNAL OFF UNDEFINEDVAR2
[cond.information.argument]

A CALL trap calls its routine with one argument, the condition object of the condition that it answers, so ARG() is 1 there and ARG(1) is a directory with the entries of the entries rule. A SIGNAL trap passes no argument: ARG() at its label is what it is at any other place of the code, which is the arguments of the routine that holds the label. That directory is the condition object itself, and none of the copies that the object rule of CONDITION says CONDITION('O') answers is the argument. The options C, D, I and A of CONDITION read the current entries of the object itself, so a change that the routine makes to its argument shows in what they answer, and in the entries of a copy made after it. The option S reads no entry, and the status rule says what it answers.

The condition object

[cond.information.object]

The condition object is a directory with these entries, whose names are in capital letters. CONDITION, DESCRIPTION, INSTRUCTION and ADDITIONAL are the entries that the object rule of CONDITION names. PACKAGE is the package that holds the code that raised the condition, and PROGRAM its name. POSITION is the number of the line on which the clause that raised the condition starts, in that code, and a NOTREADY that the interpreter raised has none. PROPAGATED is 1 when the condition left the level that raised it and 0 otherwise, as the propagated rule specifies. STACKFRAMES and TRACEBACK are lists with one item for each active level of code at that time, the main program's included, and the text of a traceback line is not specified. ADDITIONAL is present for a SYNTAX, NOMETHOD, NOSTRING or NOTREADY that the interpreter raised. A condition that a RAISE instruction raised has POSITION, and has ADDITIONAL exactly when the instruction gave one, whatever the name of the condition, as the options rule of RAISE says. The exception is a SYNTAX, which always has an ADDITIONAL array, empty when the instruction gave none, as the SYNTAX rule of RAISE says. SYNTAX adds CODE, the error number with its subcode as 41.1, RC, its major number, ERRORTEXT, the text of the error that the ERRORTEXT builtin answers for RC, and MESSAGE, the text with the details of this occurrence. ERROR and FAILURE have RC, the return code of the command. The texts of the messages are not specified, and the entry RESULT is not specified here.

      'PACKAGE', 'PROGRAM', 'PROPAGATED', 'STACKFRAMES', 'TRACEBACK')

      'POSITION', 'RC')
    if o~hasIndex(k) then line = line k
  end

  return

For a SYNTAX condition, CODE is the string m.n of the error number and subcode, RC is m, ERRORTEXT equals what the ERRORTEXT builtin answers for RC, PACKAGE is the package that .CONTEXT~PACKAGE answers in the code that raised it, PROGRAM is the name of that package, and POSITION is the line of the clause, and PROPAGATED is 0 when the code that raised it answers it, as the propagated rule says for the other case. ADDITIONAL is an array of the values that the error message names, a for the nonnumeric value 'a' of error 41.1. The description of a SYNTAX condition is the null string.

signal on syntax name s
x = 1 + 'a'
s: o = condition('o')
say o~code o~rc o~position o~propagated '['o~description']'
say (o~errortext == errortext(o~rc)) (o~program == .context~package~name),
    (o~package == .context~package)
say o~additional~class o~additional~items o~additional~at(1)
say o~stackframes~class o~traceback~class

41.1 41 2 0 []
1 1 1
The Array class 1 a
The List class The List class
[cond.information.context]

In a trapped condition's code, .CONTEXT~CONDITION answers a new directory that holds the same entries as CONDITION('O'), and .nil when the code holds no record. Every call answers a new directory, so two answers are not identical and a change to one is seen by neither the other nor the builtin. The method reads the record that the scope rule of CONDITION describes, so the option R of CONDITION clears what the method reads.

say '[' || .context~condition || ']' (.context~condition == .nil)
signal on syntax name h
x = 1 + 'a'
h: c = .context~condition
say c~class c~condition c~code (c == condition('o')),
    (c~code == condition('o')~code)
say (c == .context~condition) (c~condition == .context~condition~condition)
c~condition = 'changed'
say condition('c') condition('o')~condition .context~condition~condition
say '['condition('r')']' (.context~condition == .nil) sub()
return
sub: return (.context~condition == .nil)

[The NIL object] 1
