DIGITS

DIGITS()

ANSI: 9.5.4; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > DIGITS

DIGITS answers the setting of NUMERIC DIGITS in force where it is called: the count of significant digits that arithmetic keeps.

Arguments

[bif.digits.args]

DIGITS takes no arguments. The argument count is checked by the builtin call rules: none is required and none is the most, so a call with an argument raises SYNTAX 40.4, whatever its value, while a call with only omitted places counts as a call with no arguments. DIGITS does not run as a String method: sending the message DIGITS to a string raises SYNTAX 97.1.

say digits() digits( ) digits(,)
signal on syntax name a
say digits(1)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say digits('')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say digits(, 9)
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say 9~digits
d: say condition('o')~code

9 9 9
40.4
40.4
40.4
97.1

The result

[bif.digits.result]

DIGITS answers the setting as a whole number written without a sign, a point, an exponent or leading zeros. At the start of a program the setting is the default of the package, and the NUMERIC DIGITS instruction changes it, to the value of its expression as a whole number.

say digits()
numeric digits 1e3
say digits() datatype(digits(), 'W')
numeric digits ' 0015.0 '
say digits()
numeric digits 12 + 3 * 2
say digits()

9
1000 1
15
18
[bif.digits.default]

The default of a package is 9 unless a ::OPTIONS directive of the package names another value with its DIGITS keyword. Where it does, that value is the setting at the start of the program, the setting at the start of each of its ::ROUTINE routines and methods, and the setting that the NUMERIC DIGITS instruction without an expression returns to.

say 'start' digits()
numeric digits 20
say 'set' digits()
numeric digits
say 'reset' digits() later() .holder~new~m
exit
::options digits 12
::routine later
numeric digits 30
numeric digits
return digits()
::class holder
::method m
return digits()

start 12
set 20
reset 12 12 12
[bif.digits.scope]

The setting belongs to the routine or method that is running. An internal routine, which CALL or a function call reaches by its label, starts with the setting in force at the call, and the caller's setting is unchanged when it returns, whatever it set meanwhile. A routine of a ::ROUTINE directive, public or private, a method (also one that another method sends the message to), and an external routine in another file all start with the default of their own package, whatever the setting of the caller. The NUMERIC instruction in an INTERPRET string changes the setting of the running routine, and the change stays after the INTERPRET.

numeric digits 15
say 'main' digits() inner() later() later2() .holder~new~m
call set30
say 'main' digits()
call later3
call hidden
say .holder~new~n
interpret 'numeric digits 17'
say 'main' digits()
exit
inner: return digits()
later: numeric digits 21; return digits()
set30: numeric digits 30; say 'set30' digits(); return
::routine later2
return digits()
::routine later3
say 'later3' digits()
::routine hidden private
say 'hidden' digits()
::class holder
::method m
return digits()
::method n
numeric digits 40
return self~m digits()

main 15 15 21 9 9
set30 30
main 15
later3 9
hidden 9
9 40
main 17

DIRECTORY

DIRECTORY([newdirectory])

rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > DIRECTORY

DIRECTORY answers the name of the current directory, and with an argument first makes another directory the current one. The current directory is where a relative file name starts: the stream builtins, QUALIFY and the commands the program starts all read it.

The rules here are those of a Unix-like system, where the components of a name are separated by slashes. The names of other platforms are not specified.

Note. The current directory at the start of a program belongs to whoever started it, so the examples name no directory of their own. They build their expected values from the answer of a call without an argument, or use the root directory, /, which every Unix-like system has.

Arguments

[bif.directory.args]

newdirectory is a string, and it is optional. DIRECTORY does not run as a String method: sending the message DIRECTORY to a string raises SYNTAX 97.1. It follows the native call rule, both for the number of arguments, so that DIRECTORY(,) is a call without an argument and DIRECTORY(, 'x') raises SYNTAX 88.922, and for an argument that is an object other than a string, such as .nil or .object~new.

here = directory()
signal on syntax name a
say directory('/', 'x')
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say directory(, 'x')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say directory(.nil)
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say '/'~directory
d: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name e
say directory(.object~new)
e: say condition('o')~code
signal off syntax
say (directory(,) == here) (directory() == here)
say directory(.array~of('/')) directory(.mutablebuffer~new('/usr'))

88.922
88.922
88.909
97.1
88.909
1 1
/ /usr

The result

[bif.directory.get]

A call without an argument answers the full name of the current directory and changes nothing. The name is absolute: it starts with a slash, it has no component of one or two periods, no run of slashes and no slash at the end, except that the name of the root directory is the single slash. Symbolic links in it are resolved. What a call answers after the current directory has been removed is not specified.

here = directory()
say left(here, 1) (directory() == here) (pos('//', here) = 0) (pos('/./', here || '/') = 0)
call directory '/'
say directory()
address system 'mktemp -d' with output stem t.
base = directory(t.1)
call sysmkdir base || '/real'
address system 'ln -s real' base || '/link'
say directory(base || '/link') == base || '/real'
call directory '/'
address system 'rm' base || '/link'
call sysrmdir base || '/real'
call sysrmdir base
say sysisfiledirectory(base)

/ 1 1 1
/
1
0
[bif.directory.set]

A call with an argument that names an existing directory makes that directory the current one and answers its full name, in the form of the rule above. A name that does not start with a slash is taken from the current directory. Components of one and two periods, repeated slashes and a slash at the end are allowed in the argument, and a symbolic link is followed, so the answer can differ from the argument in all of these. The change stays until another call changes it again: ending a routine does not undo it.

here = directory()
parent = directory('..')
base = filespec('N', here)
say directory('/usr/../') directory('//')
say (directory(here || '/') == here) (directory(parent || '//' || base || '/./') == here)
call sub
say directory() == '/'
call directory here
say (directory(parent) == parent) (directory(base || '/.') == here)
exit
sub: call directory '/'
return

/ /
1 1
1
1 1
[bif.directory.fail]

A call with an argument answers the null string, and leaves the current directory as it was, when the argument does not name a directory that can be made the current one: a name that no file has, a name that is a file other than a directory, a directory the program has no permission to enter, and the null string. The null string is a name, not an omitted argument, so it does not ask for the current directory. A name is taken as written: blanks at its start or end are part of it. A '00'x ends the name: the characters after it play no part.

here = directory()
say '[' || directory('/spec-directory-none') || ']' '[' || directory('') || ']'
say '[' || directory('/dev/null') || ']' '[' || directory(' /') || ']' '[' || directory('/ ') || ']'
say directory() == here
say directory('/usr' || '00'x || '/spec-directory-none') directory()

[] []
[] [] []
1
/usr /usr

Note. The example makes the directory without permission under a temporary directory of its own, and makes its own directory current again before it restores the permission and removes both. It assumes a user other than root, whom the missing permission does not keep out of the directory.

here = directory()
address system 'mktemp -d' with output stem t.
base = directory(t.1)
call directory here
d = base || '/locked'
call sysmkdir d
address system 'chmod 000' d
say '[' || directory(d) || ']' (directory() == here)
call directory here
address system 'chmod 755' d
call sysrmdir d
call sysrmdir base
say sysisfiledirectory(base)

[] 1
0
[bif.directory.home]

An argument that is ~ alone, or that starts with ~/, has that ~ replaced by the value of the environment variable HOME, and the result is taken as above. When HOME has the null string as its value, does not start with a slash or names no directory, the call answers the null string and changes nothing. What the call does when HOME has no value is not specified.

call value 'HOME', '/', 'ENVIRONMENT'
say directory('~') directory('/usr') directory('~/') directory('~//tmp')
call value 'HOME', '/spec-directory-none', 'ENVIRONMENT'
say '[' || directory('~') || ']' directory()
call value 'HOME', '', 'ENVIRONMENT'
say '[' || directory('~') || ']' directory()
call value 'HOME', 'usr', 'ENVIRONMENT'
call directory '/'
say '[' || directory('~') || ']' '[' || directory('~/lib') || ']' directory()

/ /usr / /tmp
[] /tmp
[] /tmp
[] [] /
[bif.directory.user]

An argument that starts with ~ followed by a name, such as ~user or ~user/lib, has the ~ and the name, up to the first slash or the end, replaced by the home directory of the user of that name, as the system's user database gives it; HOME plays no part. When no user has that name, or that user's home directory cannot be made the current one, the call answers the null string and changes nothing, even when the current directory holds a directory called ~user. The name ./~user reaches that directory.

here = directory()
address system 'mktemp -d' with output stem t.
base = directory(t.1)
call value 'HOME', base, 'ENVIRONMENT'
home = directory('~' || userid())
say (home \== '') (home \== base) (directory() == home)
call directory base
call sysmkdir base || '/~spec_directory_nouser'
say '[' || directory('~spec_directory_nouser') || ']' (directory() == base)
say directory('./~spec_directory_nouser') == base || '/~spec_directory_nouser'
call directory here
call sysrmdir base || '/~spec_directory_nouser'
call sysrmdir base
say sysisfiledirectory(base)

1 1 1
[] 1
1
0

What the current directory affects

[bif.directory.effect]

A change of the current directory is seen by everything that takes a relative name afterwards: QUALIFY puts the new directory in front of a relative name, a stream builtin opens a relative file name in it, and a command started with ADDRESS runs in it.

call directory '/'
say qualify('x') qualify('./y/z')
say stream('spec-directory-none.tmp', 'c', 'query exists') == ''
address system 'pwd' with output stem out.
say out.1

/x /y/z
1
/

ENDLOCAL

ENDLOCAL()

rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > ENDLOCAL (Linux only)

ENDLOCAL takes back the most recent save that SETLOCAL made: it makes the directory the current one again, and gives the environment variables the values they had when the save was made. It answers 1 when there was a save to take back and 0 when there was none.

Note. The examples use names that start with SPEC_ENDLOCAL for the environment variables they change. Each example takes at most one save back, counting the one that the reference implementation puts back at the end of a ::routine, a method or the program, because that implementation can fail in a program that takes a save back a second time. The rule on nested saves therefore has no example; a test of interrexx backs it.

Arguments

[bif.endlocal.args]

ENDLOCAL takes no argument. A call with an argument raises SYNTAX 40.4, by the call rules. A trailing omitted place adds nothing to the count, so ENDLOCAL(,) is a call without an argument. ENDLOCAL does not run as a String method: sending the message ENDLOCAL to a string raises SYNTAX 97.1.

signal on syntax name a
say endlocal(1)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say endlocal(, 'x')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say 'x'~endlocal
c: say condition('o')~code
signal off syntax
say endlocal(,)

40.4
40.4
97.1
0

The result

[bif.endlocal.none]

A call when no save is outstanding answers 0 and changes nothing: not the current directory, not an environment variable. A program that has never called SETLOCAL is in this state.

Note. In the reference implementation, a call with no save outstanding crashes the interpreter when SETLOCAL has been called earlier by the same program, ::routine or method, its internal routines and INTERPRET included. It is specified here as it is before the first SETLOCAL, and the example does not go beyond that.

here = directory()
call value 'SPEC_ENDLOCAL_A', 'a0', 'ENVIRONMENT'
say endlocal() endlocal()
say (directory() == here) value('SPEC_ENDLOCAL_A',, 'ENVIRONMENT')

0 0
1 a0
[bif.endlocal.restore]

A call when a save is outstanding takes the most recent one back and answers 1. The current directory is then the directory of the save, and each environment variable that the save held has the value it held; the environment variables that the program changed in between are therefore undone, and so is a null-string value given to one of them. The call can be in an internal routine or in code that INTERPRET runs, as the owner of a save allows. A call in a ::routine or a method does not see the saves of the code that called it: with no save of its own outstanding it answers 0, and the caller's save stays outstanding.

here = directory()
call value 'SPEC_ENDLOCAL_B', 'b0', 'ENVIRONMENT'
call value 'SPEC_ENDLOCAL_C', 'c0', 'ENVIRONMENT'
call setlocal
call value 'SPEC_ENDLOCAL_B', 'b1', 'ENVIRONMENT'
call value 'SPEC_ENDLOCAL_C', '', 'ENVIRONMENT'
call directory '/'
say directory() value('SPEC_ENDLOCAL_B',, 'ENVIRONMENT')
call sub
say (directory() == here) value('SPEC_ENDLOCAL_B',, 'ENVIRONMENT'),
    value('SPEC_ENDLOCAL_C',, 'ENVIRONMENT')
exit
sub:
say endlocal()
return

/ b1
1
1 b0 c0

call value 'SPEC_ENDLOCAL_F', 'f0', 'ENVIRONMENT'
call setlocal
call value 'SPEC_ENDLOCAL_F', 'f1', 'ENVIRONMENT'
call r
.t~new~m
say value('SPEC_ENDLOCAL_F',, 'ENVIRONMENT')
exit
::routine r
say 'routine' endlocal()
::class t
::method m
say 'method' endlocal()

routine 0
method 0
f1
[bif.endlocal.nested]

Saves are taken back one at a time, the most recent first, and a save that has been taken back is no longer outstanding: with two saves outstanding, a call takes back the second, the next call takes back the first, and a third call answers 0.

Note. The reference implementation fails on the second of these calls, so this rule has no example.

[bif.endlocal.scope]

ENDLOCAL restores only the directory and the environment variables. A variable of the program, the NUMERIC settings and the trace setting keep the values they have when ENDLOCAL is called, and an environment variable that did not exist when the save was made is not removed: it keeps the value the program gave it. The commands that the program starts afterwards see the restored environment.

call value 'SPEC_ENDLOCAL_D', 'd0', 'ENVIRONMENT'
call setlocal
call value 'SPEC_ENDLOCAL_D', 'd1', 'ENVIRONMENT'
call value 'SPEC_ENDLOCAL_E', 'e1', 'ENVIRONMENT'
x = 5
numeric digits 12
trace o
call endlocal
say x digits() trace() value('SPEC_ENDLOCAL_E',, 'ENVIRONMENT')
address system 'echo "$SPEC_ENDLOCAL_D"' with output stem out.
say out.1

5 12 O e1
d0

ERRORTEXT

ERRORTEXT(n)

ANSI: 9.5.5; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > ERRORTEXT

ERRORTEXT answers the message that goes with an error number: the sentence that names the kind of error, without the number, the program or the line.

Arguments

[bif.errortext.args]

ERRORTEXT takes one argument, n, and nothing else. The argument count is checked by the builtin call rules: one argument is required and one is the most, so a call with two raises SYNTAX 40.4, whatever the second is. ERRORTEXT does not run as a String method: sending the message ERRORTEXT to a string raises SYNTAX 97.1.

signal on syntax name a
say errortext()
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say errortext(26, 'S')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say errortext(, )
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say 16~errortext
d: say condition('o')~code

40.3
40.4
40.3
97.1
[bif.errortext.n]

n is a whole number that passes the whole-number rules, so a number such as 26.0, 2.6e1, ' 26 ' or 026 is 26. Its value must be in the range 0 to 99: a whole number outside it raises SYNTAX 40.903, -0 is 0, and a string that is not a whole number, the null string included, raises SYNTAX 40.12, as does a number whose magnitude is too large. The caller's NUMERIC DIGITS plays no part. The form is checked before the range, so a number that is both out of range and not whole, such as 100.5, raises SYNTAX 40.12.

numeric digits 1
say errortext(26) '/' errortext(26.0) '/' errortext(' 26 ') '/' errortext('026'),
    '/' errortext(2.6e1) '/' errortext(99)
say '['errortext('-0')']'
signal on syntax name a
say errortext(100)
a: say condition('o')~code

say errortext(-1)
b: say condition('o')~code

say errortext(1.5)
c: say condition('o')~code

d: say condition('o')~code

e: say condition('o')~code

say errortext(1e30)
f: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name g
say errortext(100.5)
g: say condition('o')~code

[bif.errortext.result]

For an error number n that has a message, ERRORTEXT returns the text of the message: a sentence that ends in a period, with no error number, no subcode and no values filled in. Error numbers are the major numbers of the SYNTAX conditions, and a subcode is not an argument: ERRORTEXT(40) is the text for every error 40.n. The numbers 3 to 11, 13 to 31, 33 to 49, 88 to 93 and 97 to 99 have a message, and the following lists them all.

do i = 0 to 99

[bif.errortext.condition]

The text of a number is the text that a SYNTAX condition of that major number carries as its ERRORTEXT entry, so ERRORTEXT(n) for the number rc of a trapped syntax error is the same string as the condition's own.

signal on syntax name h

FILESPEC

FILESPEC(option, filespec)

rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > FILESPEC

FILESPEC takes a file specification apart and answers one piece of it: its directory, its file name or the extension of that name. It works on the characters of the specification alone. It looks at no file, so the file need not exist, and it never asks the file system anything.

The rules here are those of a Unix-like system, where the components of a specification are separated by slashes. The specifications of other platforms, such as those with a drive letter or with backslashes, are not specified.

Arguments

[bif.filespec.args]

option is a string whose first character picks the piece, as the next rule says, and filespec is a string; both are required. FILESPEC does not run as a String method: sending the message FILESPEC to a string raises SYNTAX 97.1. It follows the native call rule, both for the number of arguments and for an argument that is an object other than a string, such as .nil.

signal on syntax name a
say filespec()
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say filespec('N')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say filespec(, 'a/b')
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say filespec('N', 'a/b', 'c')
d: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name e
say filespec('N', .nil)
e: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name f
say 'a/b'~filespec('N')
f: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name g
say filespec('N', .told~new)
g: say condition('o')~code
signal off syntax
say filespec('N', 'a/b', ) filespec(.array~of('N'), .mutablebuffer~new('a/b'))
::class told
::method string
  return 'a/b'

88.901
88.901
88.901
88.922
88.909
97.1
88.909
b b
[bif.filespec.option]

The first character of option picks the piece, in either case, and the characters after it are ignored. The pieces are Drive, Extension, Location, Name and Path, so the first character is one of D, E, L, N and P. Any other first character, and the null string, raises SYNTAX 40.904. A blank is a character: it does not pick a piece, and nothing strips it. The checks of the arguments come first, so a call with a wrong option and a wrong argument raises the error of the argument.

f = '/usr/lib/libm.so'
say filespec('Name', f) filespec('NAMEXYZ', f) filespec('n', f)
say filespec('path', f) filespec('Location', f) filespec('P', f)
say '[' || filespec('drive', f) || ']' filespec('ext', f) filespec('e', f)
signal on syntax name a
say filespec('', f)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say filespec('X', f)
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say filespec(' N', f)
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say filespec('X', .nil)
d: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name e
say filespec('X', f, 'x')
e: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name g
say filespec('X')
g: say condition('o')~code

The pieces

[bif.filespec.path]

Path is the part of filespec up to and including its last slash, and the null string when filespec has no slash. Location is the same string. A specification that ends in a slash is all path, and one that is only slashes is its own path.

say '[' || filespec('P', '/usr/lib/libm.so') || ']' '[' || filespec('L', 'a/b') || ']'
say '[' || filespec('P', 'libm.so') || ']' '[' || filespec('L', 'libm.so') || ']'
say '[' || filespec('P', '/usr/lib/') || ']' '[' || filespec('P', 'a/b/') || ']'
say '[' || filespec('P', '/') || ']' '[' || filespec('L', '//') || ']'
say '[' || filespec('P', '/x') || ']' '[' || filespec('P', 'a//b') || ']'

[/usr/lib/] [a/]
[] []
[/usr/lib/] [a/b/]
[/] [//]
[/] [a//]
[bif.filespec.name]

Name is the part of filespec after its last slash. It is the whole of filespec when there is no slash, and the null string when filespec ends in a slash. A name of periods, such as . or .., is a name like another. A '00'x ends filespec: every piece is taken from the characters before the first '00'x, and the characters from it on are part of no piece. A line feed, a tab and every other character are ordinary characters. The path and the name together are filespec up to its first '00'x, with nothing lost between them.

say '[' || filespec('N', '/usr/lib/libm.so') || ']' '[' || filespec('N', 'libm.so') || ']'
say '[' || filespec('N', '/usr/lib/') || ']' '[' || filespec('N', '/') || ']'
say '[' || filespec('N', '.') || ']' '[' || filespec('N', '/x/..') || ']'
say '[' || filespec('N', 'x y/z w') || ']' '[' || filespec('P', 'x y/z w') || ']'
r = ''
do s over .array~of('/a/b.c', 'a//b', '/', '', 'a/', ' a/b ')
  r = r (filespec('P', s) || filespec('N', s) == s)
end
say strip(r)
s = 'x/y.v' || '00'x || '/z.w'
say '[' || filespec('P', s) || ']' '[' || filespec('N', s) || ']' '[' || filespec('E', s) || ']'
say filespec('N', 'a/b' || '0a'x || 'c') == 'b' || '0a'x || 'c'

[.] [..]
[z w] [x y/]
1 1 1 1 1 1
[x/] [y.v] [v]
1
[bif.filespec.extension]

Extension is the part of the name after its last period. It is the null string when the name has no period and when its last period is its last character. A period that starts the name counts like any other, so a name that is only an extension has it as its extension. Periods in the path before the name play no part.

say '[' || filespec('E', 'libm.so') || ']' '[' || filespec('E', 'a.b.c') || ']'
say '[' || filespec('E', 'archive.tar.gz') || ']' '[' || filespec('E', '/x/.hidden') || ']'
say '[' || filespec('E', 'noext') || ']' '[' || filespec('E', 'dot.') || ']'
say '[' || filespec('E', '/a.b/c') || ']' '[' || filespec('E', 'a.b/') || ']'
say '[' || filespec('E', '/a/b.c.') || ']' '[' || filespec('E', '..x') || ']'
say '[' || filespec('E', 'x/b.c d') || ']' '[' || filespec('E', '.') || ']'

[so] [c]
[gz] [hidden]
[] []
[] []
[] [x]
[c d] []
[bif.filespec.drive]

Drive is the null string, whatever filespec is: a Unix-like system has no drives, and a colon or a letter that looks like a drive is part of the name.

say '[' || filespec('D', '/usr/lib') || ']' '[' || filespec('D', 'c:/x.txt') || ']'
say '[' || filespec('D', 'C:\win\f.txt') || ']' '[' || filespec('D', '') || ']'
say filespec('N', 'c:/x.txt') filespec('N', 'C:\win\f.txt')

[] []
[] []
x.txt C:\win\f.txt
[bif.filespec.null]

The null string has no pieces: every option answers the null string for it. A specification that is a number or has blanks in it is a specification like any other, taken by its string value.

r = ''
do o over .array~of('D', 'E', 'L', 'N', 'P')
  r = r || '[' || filespec(o, '') || ']'
end
say strip(r)
say filespec('N', 12) filespec('E', 1.5) filespec('N', 'a b.c d')

[][][][][]

FORM

FORM()

ANSI: 9.5.6; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > FORM

FORM answers the setting of NUMERIC FORM in force where it is called: how a number written in exponent notation presents its exponent.

Arguments

[bif.form.args]

FORM takes no arguments. The argument count is checked by the builtin call rules: none is required and none is the most, so a call with an argument raises SYNTAX 40.4, whatever its value, while a call with only omitted places counts as a call with no arguments. FORM does not run as a String method: sending the message FORM to a string raises SYNTAX 97.1.

say form() form( ) form(,)
signal on syntax name a
say form(1)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say form('')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say form(, 'SCIENTIFIC')
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say 'x'~form
d: say condition('o')~code

SCIENTIFIC SCIENTIFIC SCIENTIFIC
40.4
40.4
40.4
97.1

The result

[bif.form.result]

FORM answers SCIENTIFIC or ENGINEERING, in capital letters, whatever case the NUMERIC FORM instruction wrote the keyword in. The setting at the start of a program is the default of the package. The instruction can also take its keyword from the value of an expression, with VALUE, where the value must be exactly SCIENTIFIC or ENGINEERING, in capital letters and without blanks around it, or SYNTAX 25.11 is raised and the setting stays as it was.

say form()
numeric form engineering
say form()
numeric form scientific
say form()
numeric form value 'ENGINEERING'
say form()
k = 'SCIENTIFIC'
numeric form value k
say form()
numeric form Engineering
say form()
signal on syntax name a
numeric form value ' SCIENTIFIC '
a: say condition('o')~code form()
signal on syntax name b
numeric form value 'scientific'
b: say condition('o')~code form()

SCIENTIFIC
ENGINEERING
SCIENTIFIC
ENGINEERING
SCIENTIFIC
ENGINEERING
25.11 ENGINEERING
25.11 ENGINEERING
[bif.form.default]

The default of a package is SCIENTIFIC unless a ::OPTIONS directive of the package names another value with its FORM keyword. Where it does, that value is the setting at the start of the program, the setting at the start of each of its ::ROUTINE routines and methods, and the setting that the NUMERIC FORM instruction without an expression returns to.

say 'start' form()
numeric form scientific
say 'set' form()
numeric form
say 'reset' form() later() .holder~new~m
exit
::options form engineering
::routine later
numeric form scientific
numeric form
return form()
::class holder
::method m
return form()

start ENGINEERING
set SCIENTIFIC
reset ENGINEERING ENGINEERING ENGINEERING
[bif.form.scope]

The setting belongs to the routine or method that is running. An internal routine, which CALL or a function call reaches by its label, starts with the setting in force at the call, and the caller's setting is unchanged when it returns, whatever it set meanwhile. A routine of a ::ROUTINE directive, public or private, a method (also one that another method sends the message to), and an external routine in another file all start with the default of their own package, whatever the setting of the caller. The NUMERIC instruction in an INTERPRET string changes the setting of the running routine, and the change stays after the INTERPRET.

numeric form engineering
say 'main' form() inner() later() later2() .holder~new~m
call setsci
say 'main' form()
call later3
call hidden
say .holder~new~n
interpret 'numeric form scientific'
say 'main' form()
exit
inner: return form()
later: numeric form scientific; return form()
setsci: numeric form scientific; say 'setsci' form(); return
::routine later2
return form()
::routine later3
say 'later3' form()
::routine hidden private
say 'hidden' form()
::class holder
::method m
return form()
::method n
numeric form engineering
return self~m form()

main ENGINEERING ENGINEERING SCIENTIFIC SCIENTIFIC SCIENTIFIC
setsci SCIENTIFIC
main ENGINEERING
later3 SCIENTIFIC
hidden SCIENTIFIC
SCIENTIFIC ENGINEERING
main SCIENTIFIC

FORMAT

FORMAT(number [, before [, after [, expp [, expt]]]])

ANSI: 9.4.2; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > FORMAT

Deviations: D4

FORMAT writes a number in a chosen layout: a fixed width for the integer part, a fixed count of decimal places, and a choice of when the exponent form is used and how wide its exponent is. Called with only a number it writes the number the way arithmetic would.

Arguments

[bif.format.method]

FORMAT is a builtin that runs as a String method, and number, its first argument, is the receiver; before, after, expp and expt become the message's arguments. number is a number, and each of the others is a whole-number argument that is a count of character places. The argument count is checked by the builtin call rules: one is required and five is the most.

say '['format(3.5, 4)']' '['3.5~format(4)']' '['3.5~format(4, 2)']'
signal on syntax name a
say format()
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say format(, 4)
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say format(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6)
c: say condition('o')~code

[   3.5] [   3.5] [   3.50]
40.3
40.5
40.4
[bif.format.errors]

The checks run in this order, and the first that fails is raised: the form and value of before, after, expp and expt, from left to right, which raise SYNTAX 40.12; that number is a number, SYNTAX 93.943; that none of the four counts is negative, from left to right, SYNTAX 93.906; and last the fit of the result: that the exponent has at most expp digits, SYNTAX 93.941, and then that the integer part has at most before characters, SYNTAX 93.942. The null string is not omitted and raises 40.12, and -0 is 0.

say '['format(5, ' 2 ', '-0')']'
signal on syntax name a
say format(5, , '')
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say format('x', 'y', -1)
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say format('x', -1)
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say format(5, 1, -1, -1)
d: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name e
say format(5, , 1.5)
e: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name f
say format('1e15', 0, , 1)
f: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name g
say format('1e15', 1, , 0)
g: say condition('o')~code

The result

[bif.format.default]

When only number is given, or before, after, expp and expt are all omitted, FORMAT returns the number rounded to NUMERIC DIGITS digits and written with NUMERIC DIGITS as the trigger, which is what the arithmetic of number + 0 gives.

say format('3') format(' - 48.06') format('1.50') format('00.00') format('-0')
say format('1234567890') format('0.0000000000000000001') format(5, , , , )
numeric digits 3
say format('1.2345') format('-1.2355') format('12345')

3 -48.06 1.50 0 0
1.23456789E+9 1E-19 5
1.23 -1.24 1.23E+4
[bif.format.before]

before is the width of the integer part. The integer part of the result, with its - when the number is negative, is padded on the left with blanks to before characters; when before is omitted it is not padded. The integer part is the characters before the point, or before the E when there is no point, so in plain notation a magnitude below 1 has the integer part 0. When the integer part, with its sign, is longer than before, the call raises SYNTAX 93.942. Since the integer part is never empty, a before of 0 always raises it.

say '['format(7, 3)']' '['format(-7, 3)']' '['format(0.5, 3)']',
    '['format(-12.5, 3)']' '['format(1234, 4)']'
signal on syntax name a
say format(-1234, 4)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say format(0, 0)
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say format(1, 0)
c: say condition('o')~code
say '['format(-0, 1)']' '['format(5, , 0)']'

[  7] [ -7] [  0.5] [-12.5] [1234]
93.942
93.942
93.942
[0] [5]
[bif.format.before.rounded]

The integer part that before is checked against is the one the result has, after the rounding to NUMERIC DIGITS and to after places, so a number whose rounding adds a digit to the integer part needs the room for it.

say '['format(9.4, 1, 0)']'
signal on syntax name a
say format(9.6, 1, 0)
a: say condition('o')~code
say '['format(9.6, 2, 0)']'

[9]
93.942
[10]
[bif.format.after]

after is the count of decimal places. When it is given, the number is rounded to that many places, the magnitude going up when the first dropped digit is 5 or more, or is extended with zeros to that many; and a point separates them from the integer part, unless after is 0, when there is no point. This rounding follows the rounding to NUMERIC DIGITS, and it is not limited by it, so after can ask for more places than NUMERIC DIGITS. When after is omitted, the places are those the number has. A negative number whose value rounds to zero loses its -. This book does not specify the result when the rounding to after carries the first digit to a power of ten above 999999999.

say format(123.456, , 2) format(123.456, , 5) format(123.456, , 0),
    format(-1.235, , 2) format(9.99, , 1) format(0.5, , 0)
say format(-0.4, , 0) format(-0.04, , 1) format(-0.05, , 1) format(-0, , 2)
numeric digits 3
say format(1.2345, , 6) format(12345678, , 1) format(0.12345, , 4)

123.46 123.45600 123 -1.24 10.0 1
0 0.0 -0.1 0.00
1.230000 1.2E+7 0.1230
[bif.format.trigger]

expp and expt control the notation. The trigger T of the writing rule is expt when it is given and NUMERIC DIGITS otherwise. The two counts of that rule are taken at different steps. S, the count of decimal places, is that of the number rounded to NUMERIC DIGITS, so it does not depend on after. W, the count of digits before the point, is that of the number after the rounding to after as well, so a rounding that carries into a new integer digit can make the number scientific. Which of the two tests applies is decided by the number rounded to NUMERIC DIGITS, before after is applied: a number below 1 that after then rounds up to 1 is still tested with S, and a number of 1 or more with W. An expp of 0 overrides the trigger: the result is then always in plain notation, whatever its size. With expp omitted or above 0, the number is written in scientific notation exactly when the writing rule says so for T. A T of 0 therefore makes every number scientific, zero included, unless expp is 0.

say format('12345.5', , , , 5) format('12345.5', , , , 4),
    format('0.00001234', , , , 4) format('0.00001234', , , , 3)
say format('1e30', , , 0) format('1e5', , , , 5) format('1e5', , , , 6)
say format('1e5', , , 0, 5) format('1e5', , , 3, 5) format('0.5', , , , 0)
say format('99999.5', , 0, , 5) format('99999.4', , 0, , 5),
    format('9999.96', , 1, , 4) format('99999.5', , 0, 0, 5)
say format('0.000000123', , 8, , 4) format('0.00000012', , 9, , 4)
numeric digits 3
say format('1e5') format('1e5', , , , 6) format('1.2345', , , 1, 1)
say '['format('0.999', , 0, 2, 1)']' '['format('0.999', , 0, 2, 3)']',
    '['format('1.4', , 0, 2, 1)']'

12345.5 1.23455E+4 0.00001234 1.234E-5
1000000000000000000000000000000 1E+5 100000
100000 1E+005 5E-1
1E+5 99999 1.0E+4 100000
1.23000000E-7 0.000000120
1E+5 100000 1.23
[1    ] [1] [1]
[bif.format.sci]

In scientific notation, after is the count of digits after the point in the part before the E: the digits are rounded to it or extended with zeros, as in the plain case, and with 0 there is no point. A rounding that carries into a new leading digit raises the exponent, so the part before the E keeps the form the notation gives. before is the width of the part before the point. NUMERIC FORM decides the exponent as the notation rule says.

say format('1e30', , 3) format('9.96e10', , 1) format('9.96e10', , 0),
    format('-1.2345e10', , 2)
say '['format('1.2345e10', 5, 1)']' '['format('-1.2345e-20', 3, 2)']'
numeric form engineering
say format('1.2345e10', , 1) format('1e11', 4, 1) format('9.96e10', , 1)

1.000E+30 1.0E+11 1E+11 -1.23E+10
[    1.2E+10] [ -1.23E-20]
12.3E+9  100.0E+9 99.6E+9
[bif.format.expp]

In scientific notation, expp is the width of the exponent: its digits are padded on the left with zeros to expp places, and when it needs more places, the call raises SYNTAX 93.941. The sign + or - is always written. When expp is omitted the exponent has as many digits as it needs. No such error comes from a number written in plain notation, whatever its size.

say format('1e15', , , 2) format('1e-25', , , 3) format('1e150', , , 3),
    format('1e15', , , 2, 16) format('5', , , 3, 6)
signal on syntax name a
say format('1e150', , , 2)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say format('1e-25', , , 1)
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say format('1e999999999', , , 3)
c: say condition('o')~code
say format('1e999999999', , , 9)

1E+15 1E-025 1E+150 1000000000000000 5
93.941
93.941
93.941
1E+999999999
[bif.format.exponent-zero]

A number that is to be in scientific notation but whose exponent would be 0 is written without an exponent. That number is zero, or a result, after the rounding to after, whose magnitude is at least 1 and below 10 (below 1000 under NUMERIC FORM ENGINEERING). When expp is above 0, the result then ends with expp + 2 blanks, the room the exponent would have taken; when expp is omitted nothing follows. An expp of 0 never writes the exponent, and adds no blanks.

say '['format('1.2345', , 2, , 0)']' '['format('1.2345', , 2, 2, 0)']',
    '['format('1.2345', 5, 2, 3, 0)']'
say '['format(0, , , 1, 0)']' '['format(0, 2, 1, 0, 0)']' '['format(50, , , 2, 1)']'
say '['format('-5', , , 1, 0)']' '['format('9.996', , 2, 1, 0)']'
numeric form engineering
say '['format(123, , , 2, 2)']' '['format(123, , , , 2)']' '['format(1234, , , 2, 3)']'
say '['format('-999.4', , , 1, 2)']' '['format('999.6', , 0, 1, 2)']'

[1.23] [1.23    ] [    1.23     ]
[0   ] [ 0.0] [5.0E+01]
[-5   ] [1.00E+1]
[123    ] [123] [1.234E+03]
[-999.4   ] [1E+3]

Note. The ANSI draft (9.4.2) differs from ooRexx, which this book follows, in three ways. It checks number before a count that is not a whole number, where ooRexx raises SYNTAX 40.12 for the count first (for a negative count both check number first), and it raises SYNTAX 40.13 for a negative count and SYNTAX 40.38 for a result that does not fit, in the exponent or in the integer part. It decides the notation before it rounds to after, so there a carry out of the integer part does not make the number scientific: format('99999.5', , 0, , 5) is 100000. And it tests the zeros after the point against a fixed limit, as the note on the writing rule says.

Deviations

[bif.format.deviation.4]

interrexx does not specify whether the answer of FORMAT is the same object as another string of equal value: as number itself, when the call leaves it unchanged, or as an equal string produced some other way. Through identityHash, or as a key of an IdentityTable or IdentitySet, the answer may be either, and a program can rely only on the value, which is equal under ==. ooRexx differs: it answers the argument itself in a case where interrexx may answer an equal new string.

s = '12' || '5'
say (format(s) == s) (format('125') == '125') (format(s, 5) == '  125')

1 1 1

FUZZ

FUZZ()

ANSI: 9.5.7; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > FUZZ

FUZZ answers the setting of NUMERIC FUZZ in force where it is called: the count of low-order digits that a numeric comparison ignores.

Arguments

[bif.fuzz.args]

FUZZ takes no arguments. The argument count is checked by the builtin call rules: none is required and none is the most, so a call with an argument raises SYNTAX 40.4, whatever its value, while a call with only omitted places counts as a call with no arguments. FUZZ does not run as a String method: sending the message FUZZ to a string raises SYNTAX 97.1.

say fuzz() fuzz( ) fuzz(,)
signal on syntax name a
say fuzz(1)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say fuzz('')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say fuzz(, 0)
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say 0~fuzz
d: say condition('o')~code

0 0 0
40.4
40.4
40.4
97.1

The result

[bif.fuzz.result]

FUZZ answers the setting as a whole number written without a sign, a point, an exponent or leading zeros. At the start of a program the setting is the default of the package, and the NUMERIC FUZZ instruction changes it, to the value of its expression as a whole number. A setting is a count of digits, so it must stay below the setting of NUMERIC DIGITS: both NUMERIC FUZZ and NUMERIC DIGITS raise SYNTAX 33.1 for a value that breaks this, and the settings stay as they were.

say fuzz()
numeric fuzz 3
say fuzz() datatype(fuzz(), 'W')
numeric fuzz ' 02.0 '
say fuzz()
numeric fuzz 1e1 - 7
say fuzz()
signal on syntax name a
numeric fuzz 9
a: say condition('o')~code fuzz()
signal on syntax name b
numeric digits 3
b: say condition('o')~code digits() fuzz()

0
3 1
2
3
33.1 3
33.1 9 3
[bif.fuzz.default]

The default of a package is 0 unless a ::OPTIONS directive of the package names another value with its FUZZ keyword. Where it does, that value is the setting at the start of the program, the setting at the start of each of its ::ROUTINE routines and methods, and the setting that the NUMERIC FUZZ instruction without an expression returns to.

say 'start' fuzz()
numeric fuzz 4
say 'set' fuzz()
numeric fuzz
say 'reset' fuzz() later() .holder~new~m
exit
::options fuzz 2
::routine later
numeric fuzz 5
numeric fuzz
return fuzz()
::class holder
::method m
return fuzz()

start 2
set 4
reset 2 2 2
[bif.fuzz.scope]

The setting belongs to the routine or method that is running. An internal routine, which CALL or a function call reaches by its label, starts with the setting in force at the call, and the caller's setting is unchanged when it returns, whatever it set meanwhile. A routine of a ::ROUTINE directive, public or private, a method (also one that another method sends the message to), and an external routine in another file all start with the default of their own package, whatever the setting of the caller. The NUMERIC instruction in an INTERPRET string changes the setting of the running routine, and the change stays after the INTERPRET.

numeric fuzz 2
say 'main' fuzz() inner() later() later2() .holder~new~m
call set4
say 'main' fuzz()
call later3
call hidden
say .holder~new~n
interpret 'numeric fuzz 3'
say 'main' fuzz()
exit
inner: return fuzz()
later: numeric fuzz 1; return fuzz()
set4: numeric fuzz 4; say 'set4' fuzz(); return
::routine later2
return fuzz()
::routine later3
say 'later3' fuzz()
::routine hidden private
say 'hidden' fuzz()
::class holder
::method m
return fuzz()
::method n
numeric fuzz 4
return self~m fuzz()

main 2 2 1 0 0
set4 4
main 2
later3 0
hidden 0
0 4
main 3

GC

GC([force])

rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > GC

GC asks the interpreter to reclaim the storage of objects that the program no longer reaches, and answers whether it did. A program has no need to call it: the interpreter reclaims storage on its own, and a request costs time.

This book does not specify when storage is reclaimed, in what order, or when the UNINIT method of an object runs, whether or not GC is called. A program cannot rely on any of it, and the examples show none of it. What is specified is the argument and the answer.

Arguments

[bif.gc.args]

force is optional. GC does not run as a String method: sending the message GC to a string raises SYNTAX 97.1. The call rules for the number of arguments hold: a second argument raises SYNTAX 40.4, even when the first is omitted. A trailing omitted place adds nothing to the count, so GC(,) is a call without an argument.

signal on syntax name a
say gc(, 'force')
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say gc('force', 'force')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say 'force'~gc
c: say condition('o')~code
signal off syntax
say gc(,) == gc()

40.4
40.4
97.1
1
[bif.gc.force]

force is converted to a string and must begin with the letter F, in either case: force, Force, FORCE and f are accepted, and so is any other string whose first character is F or f. Any other value raises SYNTAX 40.904: a string whose first character is something else, a blank or the digit 1 among them, the null string, and an object whose string value starts otherwise, such as .nil or .false. The argument is checked after the count of arguments.

signal on syntax name a
say gc(1)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say gc('')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say gc(' force')
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say gc(.nil)
d: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name e
say gc(.false)
e: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name f
say gc('x', 'y')
f: say condition('o')~code
signal off syntax
say gc('force') gc('Force') gc('F') gc('f') gc('fx') gc(.mutablebuffer~new('f'))

40.904
40.904
40.904
40.904
40.904
40.4
1 1 1 1 1 1

The result

[bif.gc.answer]

GC answers 1 when it reclaimed storage and 0 when it did not. A call with a valid force always reclaims, and answers 1. A call without force reclaims only on an interpreter built for debugging, which is the case when .RexxInfo~debug is true, and otherwise answers 0; in both cases the answer is the value of .RexxInfo~debug. The answer is the digit alone, 1 or 0, so it can be used as a condition.

say (gc() == .RexxInfo~debug) gc('force') datatype(gc(), 'O')
call gc
r1 = result
call gc 'force'
say (r1 == .RexxInfo~debug) result

1 1 1
1 1
[bif.gc.keeps]

A call changes nothing that the program can see: the variables, stems and objects it holds have the values they had, and the call has no other effect.

a = 'kept'
stem. = 'dflt'
stem.1 = 'one'
o = .array~of('x', 'y')
call gc 'force'
say a stem.1 stem.2 o~items o[2]

kept one dflt 2 y

INSERT

INSERT(new, target [, n [, length [, pad]]])

ANSI: 9.3.11; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > INSERT

Deviations: D4

INSERT puts a string into another string after a given character, adjusting the inserted string to a given length, and answers the combined string.

Arguments

[bif.insert.method]

INSERT is a builtin that runs as a String method, and target, its second argument, is the receiver; new, n, length and pad become the message's arguments, in that order. new and target are strings, n is a whole number of the kind the next rule describes, length is a length, and pad is a pad. The arguments are checked in the order the conventions give, and the argument count by the builtin call rules: two are required and five is the most.

say insert('123', 'abc', 1) 'abc'~insert('123', 1) '|' 'abc'~insert('123', 1, 2, '.')
signal on syntax name a
say insert('123')
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say insert('123', 'abc', 1, 1, '.', 1)
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say insert(, 'abc')
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say insert('123', , 1)
d: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name e
say insert('123', 'abc', 'x')
e: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name f
say insert('123', 'abc', 1, 1, '')
f: say condition('o')~code

a123bc a123bc | a12bc
40.3
40.4
40.5
40.5
40.12
40.23
[bif.insert.n.check]

In INSERT, n is a whole-number argument whose value must not be negative. A negative value raises SYNTAX 93.906. An n of 0 is allowed, and so is -0, which is 0. The check is a range check, and falls with those of the conventions, from left to right with the check of length.

say insert('X', 'abc', 0) insert('X', 'abc', '-0')
signal on syntax name a
say insert('X', 'abc', -1)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say insert('X', 'abc', -1, -1)
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say insert('X', 'abc', 0, -1)
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say insert('X', 'abc', -1, 'x')
d: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name e
say insert('X', 'abc', -1, 1, '**')
e: say condition('o')~code

Xabc Xabc
93.906
93.906
93.923
40.12
40.23

Note. A position elsewhere must be positive; n here counts the characters before the insertion, so 0 is its first value.

[bif.insert.n.default]

When n is omitted, it is 0: new goes before the first character of target.

say insert('45', 'xyz') insert('45', 'xyz', ) insert('45', 'xyz', , 1)

45xyz 45xyz 4xyz
[bif.insert.length.default]

When length is omitted, it is the length of new, so new is inserted whole.

say insert('45', 'xyz', 1) insert('', 'xyz', 1) insert('45', 'xyz', 1, )

x45yz xyz x45yz
[bif.insert.pad.default]

When pad is omitted, it is the blank, '20'x.

say '['insert('1', 'abc', 5, 3)']' '['insert('1', 'abc', 5, 3, )']'

[abc  1  ] [abc  1  ]

The result

[bif.insert.result]

INSERT returns the concatenation of three strings, in this order. The first is the first n characters of target, followed by as many copies of pad as it takes to make n characters when target has fewer. The second is new adjusted to exactly length characters: cut at the right when it has more, and followed by copies of pad when it has fewer. The third is the characters of target after position n, which is the null string when target has n characters or fewer. So the length of the result is length plus the larger of n and the length of target.

say insert('45', 'xyz', 3) insert('45', 'xyz', 1, 1) insert('45', 'xyz', 1, 4, '+')
say insert('45', 'xyz', 5, 6, '*') insert('45', 'xyz', , 5, '=')
say '['insert('45', 'xyz', 1, 0)']' insert('1', 'xyz', 4, 3)'.'

xyz45 x4yz x45++yz
xyz**45**** 45===xyz
[xyz] xyz 1  .
[bif.insert.past-end]

When n is greater than the length of target, the gap is filled from target's side: target is extended on the right with copies of pad to n characters, new adjusted to length follows, and nothing follows new. This holds when length is 0, so the result is then target padded to n characters.

say insert('X', 'ab', 4, 1, '.') insert('X', 'ab', 4, 3, '.') insert('xyz', 'ab', 4, 5, '.')
say insert('X', 'ab', 3, 0, '.') insert('X', 'ab', 2, 0, '.')

ab..X ab..X.. ab..xyz..
ab. ab
[bif.insert.empty]

When target is the null string, the first string is n copies of pad and the third is empty, so the result is those copies followed by new adjusted to length. When new is the null string and length is omitted, the result is target padded to n characters, and when length is given the null string new is padded to that length.

say '['insert('X', '', 0)']' '['insert('X', '', 3, 2, '.')']'
say '['insert('', 'ab', 1)']' '['insert('', 'ab', 1, 2, '.')']' '['insert('', '', 3)']'

[X] [...X.]
[ab] [a..b] [   ]
[bif.insert.length.zero]

When length is 0, the second string is the null string, whatever new is: the result is target, padded on the right to n characters when n is more than its length. pad is still checked, as a pad always is.

say '['insert('XYZ', 'ab', 1, 0)']' '['insert('XYZ', 'ab', 5, 0, '.')']'
signal on syntax name a
say insert('XYZ', 'ab', 1, 0, '')
a: say condition('o')~code

[ab] [ab...]
40.23
[bif.insert.bytes]

INSERT cuts and pads by character, one byte each, and copies every byte of new and target that stays unchanged: whitespace, control characters and '00'x are characters like any other, in the strings and as pad.

say c2x(insert('0061'x, '00'x, 1, 3, '00'x)) c2x(insert('c3a9'x, 'ff'x, 0, 1))

00006100 C3FF
[bif.insert.large]

An n or a length that is a whole number below 10**18 is valid, and a value of 10**18 or more raises SYNTAX 40.12 like any whole number that is too large. The caller's NUMERIC DIGITS setting plays no part.

signal on syntax name a
say insert('X', 'abc', 1000000000000000000)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say insert('X', 'abc', 1, 1000000000000000000)
b: say condition('o')~code
numeric digits 3
say length(insert('X', 'abc', 1234)) insert('X', 'abcdefghijkl', 1E1)

40.12
40.12
1235 abcdefghijXkl

Note. Whether, when and with which code INSERT fails for an n or a length whose result cannot be held in memory is not specified.

Note. The reference manual says that when n is greater than the length of target, new is padded at the beginning. This page follows ooRexx's behaviour, which pads target as the rule says. The ANSI draft (9.3.11) defines the third string with its SUBSTR, whose count is negative when n is at least LENGTH(target) + 1; read literally it would raise from inside the builtin where this page, like ooRexx, pads (see the note on SUBSTR).

Deviations

[bif.insert.deviation.4]

interrexx does not specify whether the answer of INSERT is the same object as another string of equal value: as target itself, when the call returns all of it unchanged as insert('', s) does, or as an equal string produced some other way, such as the literal 'abc'. Through identityHash, or as a key of an IdentityTable or IdentitySet, the answer may be either, and a program can rely only on the value, which is equal under ==. ooRexx differs: it often answers a new object where interrexx answers the existing one.

s = 'ab' || 'c'
say (insert('', s) == s) (insert('', s, 3, 0) == 'abc')

1 1

LASTPOS

LASTPOS(needle, haystack [, start [, length]])

ANSI: 9.3.12; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > LASTPOS (Last Position)

LASTPOS searches a string for another string, from the end toward the beginning, and answers the position of the first character of the last occurrence, or 0 when there is none. A starting position and a length can confine the search to a stretch of the string. POS searches from the front.

Arguments

[bif.lastpos.method]

LASTPOS is a builtin that runs as a String method, and haystack, its second argument, is the receiver; needle, start and length become the message's arguments, in that order. needle and haystack are strings, start is a position and length is a length. The arguments are checked in the order the conventions give, and the argument count by the builtin call rules: two are required and four is the most.

say lastpos('/', 'a/b/c') 'a/b/c'~lastpos('/')
signal on syntax name a
say lastpos('a')
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say lastpos('a', 'a', 1, 1, 1)
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say lastpos(, 'a')
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say lastpos('a', 'a', 0)
d: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name e
say lastpos('a', 'a', 1, -1)
e: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name f
say lastpos('a', 'a', 'x')
f: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name g
say lastpos('a', 'a', 0, 'x')
g: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name h
say lastpos('a', 'a', 0, -1)
h: say condition('o')~code

4 4
40.3
40.4
40.5
93.924
93.923
40.12
40.12
93.924
[bif.lastpos.start.default]

start is the length of haystack both when it is omitted and when it is greater than that length: the search begins at the last character either way.

say lastpos('a', 'banana') lastpos('a', 'banana', ) lastpos('a', 'banana', 6),
    lastpos('a', 'banana', 7) lastpos('a', 'banana', 999999999999999999)

6 6 6 6 6
[bif.lastpos.length.default]

When length is omitted, the search runs back to the first character of haystack.

say lastpos('b', 'banana', 6) lastpos('b', 'banana', 6, ) lastpos('b', 'banana', 6, 100)

1 1 1

The result

[bif.lastpos.result]

Let n be the length of haystack and m the length of needle. Let e be start, or n when start is omitted or greater than n. The characters that the search covers are those at the positions from e - length + 1 (or from 1, when that is less, or when length is omitted) through e; this is the window, and it holds no characters when length is 0. When m is at least 1, LASTPOS returns the greatest position k such that the m characters of haystack from position k on all lie in the window and are equal under == to needle. When there is no such k, the result is 0. A needle with no characters is the case of its own rule. The answer is written as a count, and whether it is a new object is not specified.

say lastpos('/', 'a/b/c') lastpos('/', 'abc') lastpos('ana', 'banana'),
    lastpos('aa', 'aaa') lastpos('an', 'banana')
numeric digits 3
say lastpos('x', copies('x', 1234) || 'y')

4 0 4 2 4
1234
[bif.lastpos.window]

An occurrence is found only when all of it lies in the window: a start before the end of an occurrence hides it, even when the occurrence begins at or before start, and one that begins before the window is not found. A length that would reach before the first character is cut off there, and start is limited to n before length is applied.

say lastpos('an', 'banana', 5) lastpos('an', 'banana', 4) lastpos('an', 'banana', 3),
    lastpos('an', 'banana', 2)
say lastpos('ana', 'banana', 6, 3) lastpos('ana', 'banana', 6, 2),
    lastpos('ana', 'banana', 5, 3) lastpos('ban', 'banana', 3, 2)
say lastpos('n', 'banana', 4, 2) lastpos('n', 'banana', 4, 1) lastpos('n', 'banana', 6, 3),
    lastpos('b', 'banana', 8, 6) lastpos('a', 'banana', 3, 100)

4 2 2 0
4 0 0 0
3 0 5 1 2
[bif.lastpos.length.zero]

When length is 0, the window holds no characters and the result is 0, for every needle and haystack. -0 is 0.

say lastpos('a', 'banana', 6, 0) lastpos('a', 'banana', , 0),
    lastpos('a', 'banana', 6, '-0')

0 0 0
[bif.lastpos.empty-needle]

When needle has no characters, the result is 0 for every haystack, the null string included. start and length are still checked, as a position and a length always are.

say lastpos('', 'banana') lastpos('', '') lastpos('', 'banana', 3, 2)
signal on syntax name a
say lastpos('', 'banana', 0)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say lastpos('', 'banana', 1, -1)
b: say condition('o')~code

0 0 0
93.924
93.923
[bif.lastpos.empty-haystack]

When haystack is the null string, the result is 0 for every needle and for every start and length that pass their checks.

say lastpos('a', '') lastpos('a', '', 1) lastpos('a', '', 5, 3) lastpos('', '')

0 0 0 0
[bif.lastpos.exact]

Two characters are equal only when they are the same byte. Case matters, whitespace in needle and haystack is compared like any other character, no numeric comparison is made, and '00'x and the other control characters take part like all the rest. A needle longer than haystack is never found, and neither is one that is longer than the window.

say lastpos('A', 'banana') lastpos('a b', 'a b a b') lastpos('a  b', 'a b'),
    lastpos('1', '1 01') lastpos('abc', 'ab') lastpos('ab', 'abab', 3, 2)
say lastpos('00'x, '00'x || 'a' || '00'x || 'b') lastpos('0a'x, '0a'x || 'a')

0 5 0 4 0 0
3 1
[bif.lastpos.string-form]

A needle or haystack that is a number, or an object other than a string, is replaced by its string, and LASTPOS works on the characters of that string as they are written.

say lastpos(1, '1a1') lastpos('.', 3.14) lastpos('an Object', .object~new)

3 2 1

Note. The ANSI draft (9.3.12) has no length argument, and defines LASTPOS by comparing the needle with each stretch of the haystack of its length that ends at or before start, working backward. It does not limit start to the length of the haystack: it reads the places past the end as blanks, so a needle of only blanks can be found there. ooRexx limits start first, as this book does.

LEFT

LEFT(string, length [, pad])

ANSI: 9.3.13; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > LEFT

Deviations: D4

LEFT answers the first length characters of a string, adding pad on the right when the string runs out.

Arguments

[bif.left.method]

LEFT is a builtin that runs as a String method, and string, its first argument, is the receiver; length and pad become the message's arguments, in that order. string is a string, length is a length, and pad is a pad. The arguments are checked in the order the conventions give, and the argument count by the builtin call rules: two are required and three is the most. Unlike SUBSTR, LEFT does not default length: it is a required argument, so a call without it fails by the call rules, with SYNTAX 40.3 when nothing follows its place (too few) and SYNTAX 40.5 when a pad does (missing).

say left('hi yo', 7) '|' 'hi yo'~left(7, '.')

say left('abc')
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say left('abc', 2, '.', 1)
b: say condition('o')~code

d: say condition('o')~code

e: say condition('o')~code

f: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name g
say left('abc', -1, '..')
g: say condition('o')~code

say '['left('ab', 4)']' '['left('ab', 4, )']'

The result

[bif.left.result]

LEFT returns a string of exactly length characters, the same as SUBSTR(string, 1, length, pad) returns. Its character at position i, for each i from 1 to length, is the character of string at position i when string has one, and pad otherwise. So the result is the first length characters of string, followed by as many copies of pad as make up the length.

say '['left('xy  zw', 5)']' '['left('xy  zw', 9, '.')']' '['left('pq rs', 3)']'
say '['left('abc', 3)']' '['left('abc', 1)']' '['left('abc', 5, '*')']'

[xy  z] [xy  zw...] [pq ]
[abc] [a] [abc**]
